## [REM: Lifecycle-Based Experience Memory for LLM Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27377) ⭐️ 7.0/10

REM (Reusable Experience Memory) is a framework that manages memory from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions: what to store (consolidating each completed trajectory into a phase-structured document two orders of magnitude smaller), when to recall (injecting the document at task start while withholding the costlier implementation record until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling), and what to forget (evicting the record after a single exposure). On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM achieves 68.7% match@1 versus 55.6% for the best prior memory system and improves end-task resolution from 24.9% to 27.6% at 17% lower cost. This work argues that the bottleneck in experience reuse for coding agents is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, shifting the design focus from retrieval-only memory toward control-theoretic memory management. If validated, such lifecycle-aware memory could make long-horizon coding agents cheaper and more reliable by reusing past runs instead of re-deriving solutions. Ablating any of the three decisions (store, recall, forget) reduces task resolution, and injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory—even when oracle-retrieved—does not yield the gains, underscoring that governance matters more than retrieval. The evaluation is limited to a single repository-level bug-fixing benchmark (SWE-ContextBench Lite), and no community discussion is available to gauge independent validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: LLM coding agents complete long-horizon tasks such as repository-level bug fixing through hundreds of think-act steps, a loop in which the model reasons, calls tools, and observes results. Prior memory systems for such agents focus on retrieval—finding the most relevant past trajectory—but retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether an experience is needed, at which point, or for how long. REM instead treats memory as a lifecycle with explicit store, recall, and forget decisions made inside the loop.

## [Guided-AP corrects attribution patching errors with few exact measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27393) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Guided-AP, a method that uses a small number of exact activation-patching measurements to detect and correct systematic errors in gradient-based attribution patching estimates. On a single prompt, the correction reduces error by up to 26% across three behaviors, and over many prompts it cuts the error of average effects on factual completion by 75% to 79%. Attribution patching is a widely used cheap approximation for activation patching in mechanistic interpretability, but its estimates can be far off, and verifying each one restores the full cost. Guided-AP makes the approximation more reliable at modest extra cost, which could improve circuit discovery and component attribution analyses for language model researchers. The method exploits error structure: on a single prompt, many components' errors share one sign, so a small exact sample yields one correction for the rest; over many prompts, components are misestimated similarly, so a few measured prompts reveal what to verify and how to correct each component's average effect. The analysis shows that choosing what to verify requires error size, while correction also requires sign.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Mechanistic interpretability studies which internal components of a language model matter for a given behavior. Activation patching measures a component's causal effect by replacing its activation and observing the output change, but the cost grows with the number of components and prompts. Attribution patching approximates these effects from a single gradient pass, making it much cheaper but potentially inaccurate, so researchers often treat it as a heuristic that needs verification.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27397) analyzes post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration for text embedders across three models (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, running 161 calibration experiments. It finds that calibration outcomes range from gains to catastrophic degradation depending on the 'dose' of the update, measured as functional displacement D_func, and proposes a validation-gated abstention rule that avoids harmful selections. This work provides actionable guidance for practitioners deploying quantized embedding models in retrieval systems, showing that calibration is not universally beneficial and can severely hurt performance. The proposed validation-gated abstention mechanism offers a safety net that retains most beneficial updates while avoiding harmful ones, which is directly relevant to production RAG and search pipelines. On EmbeddingGemma, the same learning-rate grid produced in-domain NDCG@10 changes from +1.47 to -71.53 points, and a label-free cosine objective also collapsed at the same dose, indicating collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than retrieval supervision. The validation-gated rule, tested on 6 independent slates and five arms, made 0 harmful selections in 30 decisions, retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention forfeiting 11.13 pp.

## [Ask-to-Distill learns to synthesize questions for on-policy distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27450) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Ask-to-Distill, a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes a student-initialized synthesizer using a distributional surrogate reward computed from a frozen student-teacher pair, without reference answers or per-candidate student updates. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard on-policy distillation, and experiments across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks show improved average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions. This work offers a new way to automatically generate high-value training questions for on-policy distillation, potentially reducing reliance on curated real question banks and making distillation more data-efficient. It could benefit LLM training pipelines that transfer capabilities from large teachers to smaller deployable students. The surrogate reward combines teacher-student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, along with length and diversity controls; the method matches or exceeds real-bank on-policy distillation in the evaluated settings, and signal analyses show optimized questions elicit denser supervision from shorter student responses. Code, data, and models are publicly available on GitHub.

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a smaller student model by having it generate its own trajectories and then matching the teacher's probability distribution at each token, rather than only imitating fixed teacher outputs. Recent work suggests OPD can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating the view that questions act as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. This paper builds on that insight by learning to generate questions that maximize the supervision signal exposed during distillation.

## [Verifier Strength and Recoverability: Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27465) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper defines two measurable quantities—verifier strength σ (how well an automated verifier, often an LLM judge, agrees with a trusted reference verifier) and recoverability (how cheaply a bad change can be undone)—that determine when an agent platform can safely allow unattended self-improvement. It demonstrates a platform applying the rule, allowing prompt, tool, and skill edits to run unattended while keeping weight updates under human sign-off. As agent platforms begin to autonomously modify their own agents, this work provides concrete, measurable criteria to decide which parts of the self-improvement loop can run without human oversight, directly addressing a timely AI safety problem. It could influence how agent platforms design approval gates and rollback mechanisms, affecting developers deploying self-improving agents. On the platform's own approval gate, the LLM judge sometimes gave the same score regardless of input (9 of 37 settings) while reporting no error, meaning a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; two simple tests catch this failure. For recoverability, restoring a saved copy returned the agent to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, and a deployed change altered 17% of task outcomes beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Agent platforms are beginning to improve their own agents by reading execution traces, deriving changes, having an automated verifier approve them, and releasing them without a human author. LLM-as-a-judge is a common automated evaluation approach, but it can suffer from biases such as agreement bias, where the judge tends to agree with the generator. Recoverability concerns how easily a bad change can be rolled back, which is critical for safe autonomy.

## [State-Bound Runtime Assurance Layer Closes AI Agent Approval Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27480) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27480) introduces a state-bound runtime assurance layer that binds an execution allowance to the decision-relevant basis of an approval and rechecks admissibility at dispatch time. In a scripted 42-case replay, the state-bound configuration identified 15 later-invalidated approvals and held 14 affected actions before dispatch, compensating one landed effect. This work addresses the evaluation-execution gap, where approvals valid at issuance become stale after facts, evidence, policy, or authority change, a critical safety issue for AI agents in operational workflows. It offers a formal assurance model and reference architecture that could influence how enterprises govern agent commitments like payments and binds. The model separates probabilistic measurement from deterministic adjudication and distinguishes continued validity of a prior approval from a current-state policy check. The results are based on stipulated policies and event orders, not superiority over dispatch-time enforcement designs, and rely on explicit interception, ingestion, dependency, and serialization assumptions.

## [MemDev-Bench: Benchmarking Memory Systems for Code Agents on Real Repository Histories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27524) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MemDev-Bench is a new benchmark that pairs each coding task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to create controlled histories, and includes an automated pipeline that makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, yielding 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. The systematic evaluation reveals three findings: memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing; memory can cause failures when agents reuse it without reassessing applicability; and providing raw historical trajectories reduces agent steps compared to compressed memory systems. This benchmark addresses a gap in existing evaluations by providing temporally valid histories with controlled relevance, enabling reliable measurement of how memory systems affect code agents. Its findings have direct implications for designing better memory systems that preserve process information and reassess applicability, which could improve the performance of AI coding assistants on real-world software engineering tasks. The benchmark includes 4,869 historical tasks derived from 555 base tasks, with relevance annotations that control whether prior tasks are related or unrelated to the current task. The evaluation shows that unrelated history tends to increase failures, and that compressed memories often omit process information that agents can reuse when given raw trajectories.

Because the knowledge corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence; the retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains recombination of strong candidates. The evaluation uses 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench across four difficulty levels, and the paper is an arXiv preprint without community discussion.

## [When Can LLM Reasoning Reliably Reuse Intermediate Results?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27662) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27662) formalizes the conditions under which large language models can reliably reuse intermediate reasoning results across retries, providing bounds on the average number of attempts and total computation. Experiments across eight reasoning models on composite math and arithmetic tasks show that, for four DeepSeek models, average success on the second subproblem rises from 36.2% without first-subproblem context to 57.2% with its answer and 58.3% with its reasoning and answer. This work addresses a practical and underexplored problem in LLM inference efficiency: instead of restarting from scratch on each retry, models could retain correct intermediate work, potentially reducing computation for multi-step reasoning tasks. The theoretical conditions and empirical results offer guidance for designing more efficient inference pipelines and retry strategies. The paper focuses on local retries that stop when no candidate passes within the retry budget, deriving conditions for correct completion and bounding the average number of attempts; it also analyzes how checking cost and the probability of passing a check affect total computation. The reported success scores measure second-subproblem coverage and include continuations made when selection fails, and arithmetic experiments show that similar first-attempt accuracies can lead to very different coverage after repeated attempts.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models often solve problems by sampling complete solutions, but each attempt starts over, and for tasks with multiple subproblems all answers must be correct in the same attempt. Reusing intermediate results from previous attempts can avoid redundant work, but errors in those results may propagate and harm later attempts. This paper studies when such reuse is reliable and how much computation it requires, combining theoretical analysis with experiments on composite mathematics and arithmetic tasks.

## [Pairwise convolutional ranking predicts cognitive traits from small MRI samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27668) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced a pairwise convolutional ranking framework that learns directly from whole-brain T1-weighted MRI by making comparative rather than absolute predictions, achieving high accuracy in predicting performance on four spatial ability tasks even with only 108 participants. The method outperformed standard regression and pointwise deep learning baselines, and backward elimination identified both common and task-specific cortical regions. This approach addresses a key challenge in neuroimaging: predicting continuous behavioral traits from small datasets, which are common in cognitive neuroscience. By extracting meaningful information from structural MRI with limited samples, it could enable more sensitive and interpretable brain-behavior analyses, potentially impacting clinical and research applications. The framework uses pairwise comparisons during training, which may improve sample efficiency, and the study employed iterative cortical-region removal to reveal brain regions supporting individual performance. However, the sample size is small (N=108) and the method was tested only on spatial ability tasks, so generalizability to other cognitive domains remains to be established.

## [Pattern Intelligence: Unsupervised LLM-Interpreted Discovery of Payer Underpayment and Denial Patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27684) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A deployed system called Pattern Intelligence clusters healthcare claims based on their adjudication behavior—using a 130-dimensional vector of payment ratios, CARC codes, and denial signals—rather than payer or contract identity, and then uses an LLM to translate each cluster centroid into an analyst-ready description. Evaluated on two production tenants with approximately 10K and 157K claims, the system surfaces systematic underpayment and denial patterns and quantifies recoverable opportunity in dollars. Healthcare providers lose substantial revenue to systematic payer underpayments and denials, and identifying correctable patterns is largely manual and does not scale to hospital claim volumes. This work offers a scalable, unsupervised approach that could help revenue cycle teams prioritize recovery efforts and negotiate with payers more effectively. Payer and contract identity are deliberately excluded from the distance metric because they dominate the geometry and collapse clusters into trivial per-payer groups; they are reintroduced only as post-hoc segmentation by contract and visit type. The system uses HDBSCAN clustering with second-pass sub-clustering on the noise set and confidence gating, and the authors report that roughly one-third to one-half of high-dollar denials form an irreducible long tail that no density-clustering configuration groups—a domain property rather than a modeling deficiency.

HDBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that identifies meaningful clusters in complex data without requiring a preset number of clusters.

## [Fine-tuning objectives shape layer-wise representations in LLM hallucination detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27711) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27711) shows that classifier-head fine-tuning (cls) consistently outperforms sequence-to-sequence LLM-as-Judge (s2s) on binary hallucination detection because cls learns a discriminative direction that reorganizes hidden states into two clear clusters, while s2s stays close to the pretrained backbone. The authors identify an 'InfoWindow' in the upper-middle layers where task information emerges, and truncating 31% of the network above this window leaves accuracy unchanged on Qwen3-4B and 8B while cutting latency by 1.4x. This work provides a mechanistic explanation for why simple classifier-head fine-tuning can beat more complex LLM-as-Judge approaches for hallucination detection, offering practitioners a principled way to design more efficient task-specific models. The finding that a fixed depth fraction transfers across models (Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B-v0.3) and tasks (QNLI, SST-2) suggests a general layer-wise structure that could guide model compression and architecture design. The cls signal saturates before the final layer, with upper layers forming a redundant plateau, but endpoint redundancy alone does not prove dispensability; training-dynamics analysis reveals a lower pretrained substrate, a narrow upper-middle InfoWindow, and a later-synchronizing upper plateau. The 31% truncation was fixed before analyzing target models and transfers across architectures and datasets, though the study focuses on binary hallucination detection and may not generalize to other task types.

**Background**: Hallucination detection in LLMs aims to identify when a model generates false or unsupported content. Two common fine-tuning approaches are classifier-head fine-tuning (cls), which adds a classification head on top of hidden states, and sequence-to-sequence LLM-as-Judge (s2s), which uses the pretrained language-modeling head to output a judgment. Linear probing is a technique that tests whether a property is linearly decodable from hidden states, and prior work has used it to audit representations. This paper combines static representation analysis with training-dynamics analysis to explain performance differences.

A controlled study on an audited HighwayEnv testbed reveals that reported benefits of experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents are largely attributable to warmup pool selection and token effects. The paper shows that the best warmup pool out of ten yields memory gains that disappear under token-matched filler controls, and that baseline port quality can silently invert conclusions. It is likely to influence future research methodology in LLM agent evaluation and autonomous driving. The study uses ten disjoint warmup pools, token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, and caution-pricing metrics. It finds that no retrieval design exceeds token-matched filler, and representational sophistication is not robustly operative; the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches are released.

## [New metric k* reveals how few features language models need for tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27724) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a readout-sparsity metric k*, defined as the smallest feature count that recovers 95% of a dense linear probe's AUROC above chance, and evaluates it on 19 language models from five labs across 14 core tasks. It finds that ten base models assign similar feature counts and nearly the same ordering to the nine reliably readable tasks, and that instruction tuning selectively reduces k*. This work distinguishes task readability from readout sparsity, offering a complementary lens for predicting how many labels a student model needs and for diagnosing changes after continual learning or pruning. It matters to mechanistic interpretability researchers and practitioners who rely on linear probes to understand and monitor language model representations. The selected features show cross-model response correspondence on three tasks beyond class-mean differences and a label-correlation-matched null, and controlled synthetic experiments show learned targets admit single-feature readouts while readable controls require tens of features. Reference-model k* is associated with label requirements across eight students following N* ∝ (k*)^0.65, and after continual learning saved heads can fail while linear readability remains high.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Linear probes are small linear classifiers trained on frozen internal activations of a neural network to test whether a property, such as a task label, is linearly decodable from representations. Dense probes use all features and measure readability via AUROC, but they do not indicate how many features are actually needed for prediction. This paper fills that gap with k*, a sparsity metric that quantifies the minimal feature set sufficient for near-dense performance.

## [Give the Model a Finger: Developmental Counting Evaluation for VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27756) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a training-free agent loop that equips vision-language models with simple image-marking tools, turning their counting process into an interpretable serial procedure. It evaluates 9 models on 682 images across 7 harness conditions using developmental counting principles, classifying each tag as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted. This work shifts focus from improving counting accuracy to auditing the serial visual reasoning process, offering a novel measurement framework that could spur follow-up work on interpretability and developmental evaluation of VLMs. It reveals model-specific exact-counting ranges spanning nearly two orders of magnitude, highlighting fundamental limitations in current vision-language models. The exact-counting range (R80) varies from 3 to 150 dots across models, and as an intervention the marking mostly fails: tags help only 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs and rarely beat verbal routines or blind point lists. However, as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows precise pointers read answers off tags, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags.

## [CrystalAR: Autoregressive Framework for Symmetry-Aware Crystal Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27762) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CrystalAR introduces a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence, reformulating continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions. The model autoregressively refines positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration, enabling constraint-aware search over both templates and geometric realizations. This approach addresses the combinatorial complexity and discrete-continuous tension in symmetry-aware crystal generation, retaining strong symmetry-template generation while achieving competitive de novo generation and template-free crystal structure prediction. It offers a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving materials discovery, relevant to AI-driven materials science. CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions conditioned on symmetry, refining all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels. This discrete hierarchical formulation enables constraint-aware search over crystallographic templates and geometric realizations, though the abstract does not specify quantitative benchmarks or limitations.

Generative models for crystals often incorporate space-group symmetry to improve realism, but introducing symmetry templates increases combinatorial complexity and creates tension between exploring discrete templates and realizing them as continuous 3D structures. ## [RITE Benchmark Tests LLM Agents' Resilience to Silent Tool Errors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27777) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces RITE, a benchmark of 167 matched units built from human-authored industrial e-commerce workflows and production-log-derived inputs, designed to evaluate whether tool-using LLM agents can recover from silent intermediate tool errors and still complete the original query. The benchmark contains 501 instances across nine workflows, covering silent-error, correct-value, and explicit-failure conditions, and tests 10 recent LLMs. Silent tool errors—where a tool returns a plausible but incorrect value without an explicit failure signal—are a practical and understudied failure mode in agentic pipelines, and the finding that they roughly halve task success across 10 LLMs highlights a significant reliability gap for e-commerce and other tool-using applications. The benchmark provides a controlled, reproducible way to measure end-to-end resilience and identify bottlenecks in error recognition, verification, and evidence integration. The benchmark uses a semantic error taxonomy to inject errors into fixed workflow prefixes, freezes recorded tool behavior for reproducibility, and lets agents continue freely; it also proposes a light State Checker as an intervention to test whether resilience can be improved. Recognition, use of an available verification path, and integration of the resulting evidence are identified as successive bottlenecks.

**Background**: Tool-using LLM agents answer queries by making multi-step calls to external tools such as APIs or databases. In production, a tool's expected output can shift between development and execution, so it may return a plausible but incorrect value without raising an error—a silent error. Such errors can propagate through subsequent agent decisions into final answers, making end-to-end resilience a key challenge for reliable agentic systems.

## [GRADUS synthesizes graded tasks from environment's latent syllabus for LLM agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27781) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GRADUS introduces a task synthesis method that treats a fixed policy-constrained environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators and composing them into increasingly difficult tasks without seed tasks or immediate-solvability filtering. It jointly calibrates tasks and solutions using execution feedback as a recovery signal, lifting a 30B model from 59% to 89% on τ²-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer. This addresses a real bias in existing agent training pipelines where only immediately solvable tasks are retained, causing training data to skew toward easier behaviors. By controlling which behaviors are explored and which survive into verified training data, GRADUS could improve how LLM agents learn policy-constrained tool use, affecting agent research and reinforcement learning for tool environments. GRADUS decouples what a task should teach from the concrete task and solution, using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations and preserving difficult examples rather than filtering them out. With an open-weight Qwen3-235B proposer, the curriculum still reaches 76% on τ²-Bench and 62% on CAR-Bench, showing the method works beyond a single strong proprietary proposer.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are models that interact with tools and backends to complete tasks, and training them often requires many example tasks that exercise environment rules. Policy-constrained environments, such as an airline backend with booking, refund, and cancellation rules, require tasks that test rules individually and in combination. Existing synthesis pipelines let a model propose tasks and keep only those it can already solve, which biases training toward easier behaviors. GRADUS instead models environment rules as guarded behavioral operators and composes them into a graded curriculum.

Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show it mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared with SFT and runs at least 4.7× faster per training step than online OPD. This addresses a key bottleneck in scaling LLM agent training: the need for large collections of executable environments, which are costly to build and maintain. By reusing existing offline trajectories without new environment observations or multi-turn interactions, SAPD could make agent training more accessible and efficient. SAPD allows the student to generate responses conditioned on recorded histories and requires neither new environment observations nor additional multi-turn interactions. The method improves performance across different teacher configurations, but it is an arXiv preprint and the code is not yet released.

**Background**: Training LLM agents typically relies on online reinforcement learning, which requires real-time interaction with executable environments, or supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline data, which can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously learned capabilities. On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training paradigm where a student model learns from dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher policy applied to trajectories sampled from the student's own policy. SAPD combines ideas from offline RL and on-policy distillation to learn from fixed offline trajectories without environment interaction.

## [Differentiable Graph Implicit Solver for PDE-Constrained Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27888) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that treats PDEs on unstructured grids as constraints, and evaluates it on four tasks: forward modeling of linear/nonlinear evolutionary and static problems, inverse estimation of equation coefficients, inverse estimation of the right-hand side, and learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. This work bridges scientific machine learning and classical numerical methods by making implicit PDE solvers differentiable end-to-end, which could significantly reduce the complexity of forward modeling while enabling efficient inverse problems—particularly valuable in geophysics where inverse problems are routinely solved to reduce model uncertainty. The solver's stability and differentiability are key enablers for complexity reduction, and the learnable graph coarsening component is used specifically to accelerate forward modeling; however, the abstract does not report quantitative accuracy or speedup results, and the approach is demonstrated on unstructured-grid problems rather than structured meshes.

**Background**: PDE-constrained optimization involves optimizing parameters or inputs of a system governed by partial differential equations, which often requires solving large, stiff linear systems. Automatic differentiation computes exact gradients through numerical operations, and when applied to implicit solvers it enables gradient-based inverse problems. Graph-based representations allow PDEs on irregular, unstructured grids to be handled with graph neural network techniques, while graph coarsening reduces graph size by merging nodes into supernodes to lower computational cost.

## [ACE-Compression: Ability-Centric Evaluation for Compressed LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27913) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ACE-Compression introduces an ability-centric evaluation framework that probes four deployment-facing dimensions—procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency—to reveal which core abilities survive or collapse in compressed large language models. The framework was tested on over 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs, covering both quantization and pruning. Standard compression evaluation only measures retained task performance, which misses the fact that compression perturbs distributed knowledge and can silently degrade specific abilities. This framework enables deployers to choose compression methods based on the ability profile their application requires, rather than just leaderboard averages, and gives algorithm designers diagnostic signals to preserve what matters. The study finds that compression redistributes ability profiles: coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical significance of this gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires.

Quantum-JEPA introduces a conditional quantum Born prior within a latent-action JEPA framework to learn distributions of future representations, where circuit measurements generate binary latent actions that a shared predictor maps to alternative futures. The model is trained via a sampled energy objective and validated on multimodal tasks, including D3IL, where it generates multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. This work demonstrates a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction, showing that quantum priors can match or improve upon variational baselines while being parameter-efficient. It opens a path toward quantum-enhanced world models and provides a basis for exploring larger-scale integration of quantum generative models in AI. The quantum prior avoids an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions, and the authors validate finite-shot parameter-shift training including readout noise. Unlike most prior work focused on simulation, they also verify inference feasibility on a real QPU.

## [ReTrace: New Framework Evaluates Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27954) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework that formalizes Transition-Consistent Recovery and uses goal-oriented action replay after controlled error injection to systematically study how computer-use agents recover from failures. It presents the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, showing that ideal recovery can unlock latent task completion capabilities, but current agents fail to exploit them. Recovery is critical for long-horizon automation where errors accumulate and actions leave side effects, yet existing remedies like environment resets, action replay, and API rollback are often infeasible or limited. This work establishes recovery as a fundamental capability and provides a tool to measure and improve reliability of computer-use agents, impacting AI/ML and systems research. Transition-Consistent Recovery requires that identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states yield identical outcomes, operationalized via goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. The study reveals that accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains, and code and dataset are available on GitHub.

## [RSOD Framework Builds Deployable Telecom LLM from Six Specialist LoRA Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27993) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD), an end-to-end framework that generates 212,559 source-grounded telecom training records across 14 networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers on a shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates them into a single student adapter called Llama-CalixCLM v1. On 2,850 held-out questions, the consolidated student scores 21.7112/25 micro, nearly matching the combined six-teacher system's 21.7641/25 and far exceeding the base Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct's 12.8661/25. This work shows that multiple domain-specialist LoRA teachers can be distilled into one deployable adapter without meaningful performance loss, addressing the practical challenge of serving many specialist models in telecom networking. The approach could lower deployment costs and simplify maintenance for domain-specific LLM applications in routing, broadband, access technologies, and operational diagnostics. RSOD uses student-generated trajectories, exact-token teacher forcing, and shared-head hidden-state reconstruction, achieving a mean absolute logit error of 7.26×10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. The 2,000-step run on four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs produced 16,000 trajectories with zero student-version or token-ID mismatches, and under a neutral deployment-like prompt the student still scores 20.0028/25 micro.

## [Dancing Diffusion turns denoising trajectory into a programmable latent program](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28003) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Dancing Diffusion introduces a latent program that assigns each span of timesteps a dedicated continuous condition block, turning conditioning into a programmable sequence. A compiler maps text features into this program, and a fixed pretrained generator executes the blocks over successive sampling intervals, allowing the trajectory to be redirected while preserving executed history. This approach enables fine-grained image editing by reusing a shared prefix and rewriting later operations without regenerating from noise, potentially influencing controllable generation research. It lays a foundation for structured intermediate computation in diffusion models, moving beyond single-instruction conditioning. On SANA, reusing an executed prefix preserves markedly more of the scene than regenerating from noise at a similar edit strength, and learned conditions preserve more background than native prompt switching. However, later branches weaken the edit, leaving semantic control over individual operations limited.

Step-level credit assignment is simplified to a binary classification of whether each step is necessary, with labels obtained via counterfactual verification to identify redundant steps.

## [Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28074) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Slot-JEPA proposes decomposing dense patch representations in JEPA world models into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks, creating a reusable object-structured prediction interface. It introduces a Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) and uses Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate plans, improving goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm tasks on REALM-JEPA. This work directly addresses three concrete limitations of JEPA latent world models—patch redundancy, missing entity correspondence across time, and displacement-insensitive pointwise losses—by providing a reusable object-centric interface that is pretrained once and frozen downstream. It could benefit the representation learning and world-model communities by making downstream predictors more sample-efficient and better aligned with spatial progress in planning. The slot decomposition is pretrained once and frozen for downstream tasks, and the TMP stores visual transitions as compact masks while retrieving context via slot statistics, with two branches separating slot-specific and shared cross-slot dynamics. The slot-reconstructed features remain transferable across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, though the work is a single arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

The paper proposes a message passing scheme directly on Structural Causal Models (SCMs) using finite-dimensional function spaces and B-spline bases, enabling unified observational, interventional, and counterfactual inference. Forward propagation combines a numerical realization of the Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS) with spline projection to recover densities, while backward message passing handles conditioning. It could impact probabilistic inference and causal reasoning by providing a systematic way to perform all three levels of causal hierarchy within a single computational scheme. The algorithm uses tensor-product B-spline bases to express inference through numerical quadrature and linear algebra without explicitly constructing conditional distributions. Experiments on randomly generated continuous SCMs show accurate approximation of Monte Carlo reference solutions and systematic improvement with increasing basis resolution.

The paper proposes SCIB, a robust learning objective for spiking neural networks (SNNs) based on the Conditional Information Bottleneck, which replaces the standard mutual information compression term I(X;S) with the conditional mutual information I(X;S|Y) and introduces a learnable class-conditional prior. Experiments on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 show improved robustness against environmental noise, hardware noise, and adversarial attacks, plus a 24.9% reduction in SynOps-based inference energy compared to an unconstrained SNN baseline. SNNs are promising for low-power neuromorphic computing but remain vulnerable to perturbations and noise, limiting real-world deployment. SCIB addresses this by improving robustness without adversarial training, which could make SNNs more practical for energy-efficient and reliable edge AI and neuromorphic hardware. SCIB derives a tractable variational upper bound for the conditional information bottleneck and uses a learnable class-conditional prior instead of an isotropic Gaussian prior to encourage class-structured representations. The energy savings are measured via SynOps, and robustness gains are observed under most evaluated noise conditions, though the abstract does not specify performance under all possible attacks.

## [FALCA: Falsification-Aware RL with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28361) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FALCA introduces a falsification-aware reinforcement learning framework that casts deep search as a propose-falsify process, using a collaborative Searcher-Falsifier architecture where independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence and produce falsification reports to revise the research state. It combines SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL based on parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions, and experiments on five search benchmarks show improved long-horizon deep search performance over backbone and harness ablations. Error accumulation is a central failure mode for long-horizon LLM search agents, where early anchoring on a wrong candidate can misguide all subsequent reasoning. FALCA's explicit falsification loop and hierarchical credit assignment offer a principled way to reduce confirmation bias, which could improve the reliability of research-oriented agents used in evidence gathering and decision support. The framework separates answer proposal from falsification by using independent Falsifiers that check unmet constraints and identify conflicts, and its RL training assigns credit at three granularities: research stages, state transitions, and actions. Evaluation covers five search benchmarks and compares against backbone and harness ablations, though the abstract does not report specific numeric gains or computational overhead.

## [RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression via Query-Key Activation Energy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28385) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RACE is a post-training method that natively reduces attention head dimensions by selecting complete rotary pairs based on joint query-key activation energy, eliminating runtime reconstruction. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, it cuts total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, boosts throughput 1.79x, lowers TTFT by 43.2%, and reduces GPU memory by 28.1% versus an uncompressed model. KV-cache memory and decoding FLOPs are major bottlenecks for long-context LLM inference, and RACE avoids the reconstruction overhead of prior compression methods while remaining compatible with RoPE. This makes it a practical, kernel-free optimization that could be folded into existing models to improve serving efficiency. The method theoretically proves that RoPE compatibility holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained, and its selection criterion minimizes a calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into model weights, requiring no runtime reconstruction or specialized kernels, and RACE outperforms structured pruning while remaining competitive with reconstruction-based methods across three model families.

The paper introduces Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA), a unified framework that combines deterministic top-k retrieval with score-guided sampling of the residual attention mass, correcting for inclusion probabilities. This matters for researchers and engineers working on efficient long-context inference across model sizes from 3B to 27B. SSA is evaluated across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME on five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, consistently improving over baselines at matched sparsity. At 50x sparsity on RULER-HARD, it recovers 94% and 85% of dense-attention performance at 32K and 128K respectively, and the code is open-sourced at the provided GitHub repository.

This work shows that LLM-driven evolutionary search can automate that design and transfer improvements across multiple datasets, potentially lowering the manual effort needed to build strong GR systems. The framework uses a locally served open-weight 31B model to mutate executable GR components, avoiding proprietary LLM APIs, and validates proxy reliability on 21 SID programs on NQ320K. ## [CoRAL: Hybrid Diffusion-Autoregressive Framework for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28584) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CoRAL introduces an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture where a diffusion language model (DLM) planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, and a large autoregressive model (ARM) executor selects the best plan and synthesizes the final answer. It also proposes Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC) to train the planner with outcome-based rewards, and experiments on vision-language benchmarks show it outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and is competitive with strong ARMs. This work tackles the sequentiality bottleneck of autoregressive models by combining the parallelism of diffusion models with the semantic coherence of ARMs, potentially enabling faster and higher-quality multimodal reasoning. If validated, the hybrid approach could influence the design of efficient LLM inference systems and reduce latency for complex reasoning tasks. The framework uses a DLM planner to generate K parallel trajectories and an ARM executor for selection and synthesis, with RDC integrating outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process. As an arXiv preprint, it lacks peer review, and the abstract does not specify the model sizes, K values, or detailed benchmark results.

## [Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction Dynamically Tunes Speculation Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28619) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP), an online control method that dynamically selects the speculation horizon for multi-token prediction based on verification feedback, improving decoding efficiency without retraining. Evaluated on five draft-target pairings with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings. This work addresses a key inefficiency in multi-token prediction: the optimal speculation horizon varies by context, and fixed horizons can waste compute. By learning to adapt the horizon online without retraining, AMTP offers a practical way to accelerate LLM inference across different model architectures and tasks, potentially benefiting deployment scenarios where latency matters. AMTP uses acceptance survival—the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted—to predict how far the draft will survive and selects the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second. Theoretically, the prediction error of any online learner translates into throughput regret against the best horizon, and with online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear, bounding wall-clock completion time.

**Background**: Multi-token prediction (MTP) accelerates language-model decoding by drafting several tokens ahead and verifying them in a single target-model pass, similar to speculative decoding. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the number of tokens to draft (the horizon) before drafting because all prediction heads fire in the same forward pass. Choosing this horizon is challenging because longer drafts amortize cost when reliable but waste compute on rejected suffixes.

## [GRaSP: Latency-Aware Re-Scoring for Geo-Distributed RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26938) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GRaSP introduces a drop-in re-scoring layer for geo-distributed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that balances relevance, latency, and cost without retraining. The paper formalizes the Geo-RAG Selection Problem, proves it is solvable optimally by an O(N log N) greedy algorithm over a partition matroid, and validates on a five-node CloudLab testbed, reducing P90 fetch latency by 41% while retaining 78% of relevance-only recall. As RAG systems are increasingly deployed across geo-distributed cloud and edge infrastructures, ignoring data location inflates tail latency and egress costs. GRaSP offers a practical, theoretically grounded solution that practitioners can adopt without retraining, making RAG deployments more efficient and cost-effective. The base formulation is a linear objective over a partition matroid, solved optimally by a greedy algorithm; NP-hardness only arises under an additive egress budget. On a CloudLab testbed emulating a four-region WAN over the Natural Questions corpus (2.68M passages), GRaSP lowers P90 fetch latency by 41% at a moderate latency setting, with sub-millisecond selection overhead stable to 200 queries/s, and reduces end-to-end context-fetch latency by 43% while staying within 0.062 absolute EM of relevance-only retrieval.

## [3D-MoE: Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26991) ⭐️ 7.0/10

3D-MoE introduces a hardware-software co-designed system that exploits 'expert complementarity'—offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps—to balance expert loads during Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decode on 3D-stacked near-memory processing (NMP) hardware. It combines offline complementarity-guided grouping, a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) for residual hotspots, and cost-aware online remapping, achieving an average 4.63× MoE-layer speedup over expert parallelism and 1.58×–1.86× end-to-end throughput improvement over the strongest NMP baselines with only 2.11% additional logic-die area. MoE decode is highly memory-bound and suffers from skewed, time-varying expert loads, making it a critical bottleneck for efficient LLM inference. This work shows that co-designing software scheduling with 3D-stacked NMP hardware can substantially improve throughput without large area overhead, which could influence future AI accelerator architectures for MoE serving. The approach first uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to achieve coarse-grained inter-group balance, then handles intra-group hotspots via a CMN that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and finally applies cost-aware online remapping to tolerate workload drift. The reported gains are averaged across MoE models, with only 2.11% extra logic-die area.

Researchers introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method that clusters activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, building a bank of latent exploration vectors that are applied to subsequent rollouts. ## [Selection Bias Flaw Found in Differential Privacy Audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27021) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27021) reveals that many differential privacy audits using membership inference attacks introduce selection bias, leading to statistically invalid and overestimated lower bounds on privacy leakage. The authors propose correction methods from statistical literature and show that without correction, audits violate theoretical upper bounds up to four times more often than their claimed confidence level implies. This work matters because flawed statistical assessments can cause false alarms on correct mechanisms or misjudge how tight a privacy guarantee is, affecting researchers and practitioners who rely on audits to validate differential privacy implementations. It highlights a subtle but important issue in privacy auditing methodology that has gone unnoticed due to most audits not being tight. The paper employs statistical tools to correct selection bias and provides an overview of different correction methods with their advantages. A comprehensive re-analysis of prior audit results shows that with correction applied, the resulting lower bounds become statistically valid and violations occur at no more than the nominal rate.

The paper introduces OptEP, a scalable continuous relaxation method for post-training expert pruning in Mixture-of-Experts language models. It achieves absolute accuracy gains of up to 15.05% on Qwen3-30B-A3B, 14.55% on Qwen3-235B-A22B, 11.06% on GLM-4.5-Air, and 16.20% on Mixtral-8x7B over the strongest existing baselines. MoE models reduce computation via sparse activation but still require storing all expert parameters, making deployment costly. OptEP addresses this by selecting a subset of experts that best reconstructs the original layer output, enabling significant memory savings while preserving accuracy, which is valuable for practitioners deploying large MoE models in resource-constrained environments. OptEP formulates expert pruning as a subset-selection problem and uses a continuous relaxation to optimize differentiable expert-selection variables, followed by a lightweight reconstruction-based update of the retained expert weights. The improvements are particularly pronounced under aggressive pruning, demonstrating that reconstruction-driven selection and weight adaptation can preserve substantially more performance.

## [LLMs show implicit thinking budget cuts when tasks are composed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27190) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27190) finds that language models make substantially more errors when multiple tasks are combined in a single prompt, even when each task is solved reliably in isolation. The authors attribute this to an implicit thinking budget: under composition, models use fewer tokens per task, and tasks requiring longer solution traces become more fragile. This reveals a fundamental limitation in how LLMs handle multi-task prompts, affecting prompt engineering and model evaluation. The finding that grouping tasks by fragility can reduce token usage by 43% while preserving accuracy suggests practical ways to optimize cost and performance. The degradation cannot be fully explained by error accumulation, and the effect is observed across open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than needed, wasting compute, but grouping tasks by fragility manipulates the implicit budgeting to save tokens.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27247) introduces an iterative prompt-editing procedure in which an LLM editor revises source-grounded seed prompts based on the target model's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation, substantially increasing judge-rated hallucination severity over static seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fell in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination, with later editing rounds accounting for more than half of the mean score increase. The work shows that static hallucination benchmarks can mask model-specific failures, since different prompts trigger hallucinations in different models even when average scores look similar. This has direct implications for AI safety evaluation and for how developers design adversarial stress tests and interpret cross-model benchmark comparisons. Experiments covered 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics across open-weight and closed-source models; among 219 prompts passing model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 still elicited unsupported claims, and across five models 200 curated prompts yielded similar average severity scores but pairwise Spearman correlations of only ρ=0.0387 to 0.1897, indicating low prompt-level agreement. The authors caution that curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the specific failures they expose in each model.

**Background**: Hallucination stress tests probe whether a language model produces false or unsupported content, and researchers commonly distinguish intrinsic hallucinations (contradicting the provided input context) from extrinsic hallucinations (claims that cannot be verified from the input). LLM-as-a-judge evaluation uses a large language model to score or classify another model's outputs against specified criteria, and adversarial prompt editing iteratively mutates prompts to surface weaknesses. This paper combines these ideas into a target-aware curation loop that adapts seed prompts to each model under test.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27257) analyzes 8 code models (6.7B–15B parameters) on C programs from DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS, finding that vulnerability information is more accessible as a paired relational signal (whether code A is riskier than B) than as a globally separable categorical label under linear probing. This suggests that standard vulnerability classifiers built on isolated samples may underperform because vulnerable and secure code form overlapping distributions in representation space, which has implications for AI safety monitoring and interpretability-based detection tools. ## [Symbolic Preference Labeling makes preference labels auditable via recorded derivations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27266) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method where a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses, explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each label includes a recorded derivation that allows recomputation without rerunning the language model, and the method was validated on 200 human-annotated prompts and 465 preference pairs for DPO training. This work addresses the opacity of preference labels used in alignment training, making the construction process inspectable and reproducible, which is valuable for AI safety auditing and interpretability. It distinguishes reproducibility from attribute correctness, highlighting that semantic safety still requires separate validation. On 200 prompts, the language model produced valid structured outputs for 192 prompts, with all eight parsing failures occurring in self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, DPO training across five seeds yielded mean benign refusal of 40.82% on 1,319 benign prompts resembling unsafe ones and mean toxic refusal of 84.98% on 655 toxic prompts.

## [VPFlow: Value-Predictive Planning with Imperfect World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27280) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VPFlow introduces a latent world model for offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning that is trained to predict goal-reaching value instead of future states, using a closed-form Monte Carlo return as the sole supervision signal. It pairs this value-predictive world model with a one-step flow policy and plans via evolutionary search in the policy's noise space, outperforming model-free baselines by at least 30.3 and 10.1 percentage points on 30 state and pixel OGBench datasets, respectively. This work challenges the prevailing assumption that accurate next-state prediction is necessary for effective planning, showing that value-predictive representations suffice and can even be harmed by minimizing state prediction error. It has implications for offline RL, world-model research, and test-time compute scaling, suggesting a more direct path to planning without precise dynamics models. The method replaces temporal-difference bootstrapping with a closed-form Monte Carlo return for value regression, and the imagined latents are trained to predict value rather than match future states, implicitly preventing representation collapse. Notably, VPFlow achieves superior performance despite latent prediction error being orders of magnitude larger than with state prediction, and explicitly minimizing this error lowers success rate.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) aims to learn policies that reach arbitrary goals from pre-collected datasets without reward signals, enabling skill acquisition and zero-shot adaptation. Model-based methods use learned world models to plan by imagining future trajectories, typically assuming accurate next-state prediction in pixel or latent space is required. Temporal-difference (TD) bootstrapping is a common value-learning technique that updates estimates using other estimates, while Monte Carlo returns use complete trajectory outcomes; VPFlow argues the latter is naturally available in offline goal reaching.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27301) evaluates context compaction methods on later questions across four corpora and finds that selecting sentences for the current question does not beat random deletion on future questions, while question-agnostic word-level deletion (LLMLingua-2) outperforms random sentence deletion by 12.5 points on later MultiRC questions at the same token budget. This counterintuitive finding suggests that agent memory systems should not optimize compaction solely for the immediate question, as scores on the current question do not reliably predict performance on later ones, which has direct implications for designing long-horizon LLM agents. On MultiRC, keeping sentences judged necessary for the current question raises accuracy by 11.4 points at 25% of tokens, but no such method beats random sentence deletion on later questions; LLMLingua-2's gain shrinks to 7.3 points when controlling for content-word retention, and on FEVER label accuracy can overstate what the kept text actually supports.

## [New Metric SAR Measures Shared Vulnerabilities in Model Pools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27353) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR), a novel measure of shared vulnerability in a model pool based on the attack diversity needed to exploit it. It theoretically formulates SAR as a partial set-cover problem with approximation guarantees and empirically tests vision and large language models, showing that pools distilled from DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Opus 4.6 exhibit lower systemic robustness than their parent pools. This work highlights the risk of a 'vulnerability monoculture' arising from homogeneous training pipelines and data, which could lead to catastrophic widespread compromise with few attacks. It provides a measurable target for more holistic adversarial evaluation of model populations, relevant to AI safety and foundation model deployment. SAR interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness: small values indicate a vulnerability monoculture, while large values indicate dispersed failures. The paper demonstrates a potential systemic cost of frontier-model distillation, as distilled pools show lower estimated systemic robustness than their parent pools.

**Background**: Adversarial robustness refers to a model's ability to resist being fooled by adversarial inputs. ## [LiBRA Uses Logit Fingerprints for Byzantine-Robust Client Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27357) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LiBRA proposes comparing clients by the class-conditional logit responses of their models to optimized pseudo-patterns, producing a fingerprint of C² values for C classes instead of comparing full parameter vectors. The authors instantiate LiBRA as variants of Krum, Multi-Krum, and Bulyan, and on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 with three architectures and four attacks, each variant matches its parent's robustness while ranking malicious clients within 0.006 AUC of the full parameter vector. This approach avoids parameter-vector comparisons, making Byzantine-robust selection compatible with secure aggregation, which is designed to hide individual client updates from the server. It also reduces comparison cost from O(n²d) to a much smaller fingerprint and enables comparisons across clients with different architectures, broadening the applicability of robust aggregation in privacy-preserving federated learning. The trust decision reads no client parameters and compares up to 49,090 times fewer values, at the cost of one pattern optimization per client per round. Evaluation is limited to standard datasets (Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10) under i.i.d. partitions, so performance under non-i.i.d. data and larger-scale settings remains to be tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Federated learning trains a shared model across clients without centralizing their data, but malicious clients can send poisoned updates. Byzantine-robust aggregation rules such as Krum, Multi-Krum, and Bulyan filter out suspect updates by comparing clients' parameter vectors, which requires access to every update and conflicts with secure aggregation—a cryptographic technique that prevents the server from seeing individual updates. LiBRA replaces parameter comparison with a fingerprint based on what each model computes, i.e., its class-conditional logit responses to pseudo-patterns optimized against the model.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27364) proposes a 'predictive closure' characterization of feature selection in Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA), reformulating the training objective to show that selection depends on properties of feature sets rather than individual predictability. Controlled experiments confirm that unpredictable features can be better represented when they help predict other features, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships affects the representation of others. This work addresses a known concern that JEPA might discard unpredictable but important features (e.g., a traffic light), offering a theoretical explanation for why such features can still be retained. It provides researchers in self-supervised learning with a more accurate framework for understanding and steering feature selection, potentially improving representation learning in practice. The predictive closure view agrees with earlier characterizations when features evolve independently but makes new predictions when they do not. The paper also shows that steering feature selection can be indirect: targeting one feature with an auxiliary objective or supplying it as side information to the predictor can strengthen the representation of another feature whose future values it helps predict.

The paper introduces NR-SAE, a sparse autoencoder that gives each routed expert in a Mixture-of-Experts model its own small dictionary and only activates the dictionaries selected by the frozen router. At block 15 of Gemma 4 26B-A4B, after ten million C4 training tokens across three seeds, NR-SAE explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs, outperforming a rank-addressed control (0.481), a candidate-matched control (0.458), and an architecture-matched control with randomized expert identity (0.387). It provides a controlled benchmark showing that expert-aligned dictionaries capture more variance than several baselines, which could inform future mechanistic interpretability research on large MoE models. Part of NR-SAE's advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert effectively names the subspace. However, the authors note that their implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.

MLIPS introduces a training-free technique that shares candidate key pools across layers in sparse attention, where a producer layer publishes a top-M pool larger than the attention budget K and subsequent layers select their own top-K from it. The method uses three consumer layers per producer, yielding observed accuracy changes of -1.49 to +0.29 percentage points in single runs, but more extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. The paper also characterizes recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers, motivating an exploratory Top-G bounded pool construction for prefill whose deployment and accuracy remain open.

The paper introduces Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm that efficiently identifies Pareto-optimal LLMs in multi-objective arena evaluations. ## [Projected Distillation Edits Failed Attempts to Learn Hard Problems On-Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27467) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.27467) proposes projected distillation, a method that minimally edits a student model's failed attempts into correct targets using contrastive updates, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. The method is evaluated on Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B across five domains (math, code, science, tool use), achieving the highest area under the specialization-retention frontier in 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and on-policy distillation (OPD), and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA. This work addresses a key limitation of on-policy reinforcement learning and distillation: the lack of learning signal on hard problems where all attempts fail, while also mitigating the capability erosion caused by off-policy targets. It offers a principled way to balance specialization on hard tasks with retention of existing capabilities, which is important for LLM post-training. Theoretically, the student's learning regret grows with edit size: linearly with the horizon under minimal correction (as in DAgger) and quadratically under full-answer replacement (as in behavior cloning). Ablations show that moving targets farther off-policy worsens the specialization-retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions, highlighting the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.27470) proposes a DCGAN-based model inversion attack on federated learning systems for large-scale medical imaging, and evaluates client-side differential privacy as a defense. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that the attack can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, and that personalized federated learning helps recover accuracy lost under differential privacy. ## [EmbGA: Genetic Algorithm Recovers Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27473) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers visual concepts present in generated images but absent from their prompts. It outperforms six optimizers on two benchmarks, achieving the highest alignment with a large exploration budget and recovering the most grounded tokens on natural images while running much faster than language-model-guided search. This work addresses a critical safety and auditing problem: text-to-image models can be implanted with hidden associations that ordinary prompts trigger, and EmbGA provides a practical tool to detect such omitted concepts. It enables researchers and auditors to uncover concealed behaviors, supporting transparency and accountability in generative models. EmbGA maintains a population of token embeddings and applies crossover by interpolating between parent embeddings and mutation by moving an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, ensuring every candidate is a valid token sequence; it is evaluated against six optimizers under two exploration budgets.

## [Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning Removes Dual-Use Risks Without Harming Benign Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27490) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a framework that uses singular value decomposition on activation covariances to define a capability subspace and restricts parameter updates to its orthogonal null space. OBU comes in two forms—Projected LoRA and Closed-Form Weight Surgery—and was tested on Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B, achieving strong separation of hazardous dual-use concepts while preserving benign domain competence. This work addresses a critical AI safety challenge: removing hazardous capabilities like cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement from LLMs without degrading legitimate scientific utility, a problem known as concept bleeding. By mathematically guaranteeing zero perturbation to benign representations, OBU could enable safer deployment of open-weight models in dual-use domains such as biosecurity and cybersecurity. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via SVD on empirical activation covariances, then restricts updates to the orthogonal null space, guaranteeing zero parameter perturbation along the calibration subspace. The Closed-Form Weight Surgery variant edits weights analytically in a single step without training, and experiments show durable resistance to adversarial relearning and mitigation of in-context priming attacks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Machine unlearning aims to remove specific knowledge or capabilities from trained models without full retraining, but in dual-use domains, benign and malicious content share vocabulary and internal representations, causing standard methods to damage benign capabilities (concept bleeding). Singular value decomposition (SVD) is a linear algebra technique that factorizes a matrix into rotation, scaling, and rotation components, often used to identify principal directions in activation space. Null space methods constrain updates to directions that do not affect protected representations, and have been explored in related editing frameworks such as X-Edit and Batman.

## [RSD: Self-Evolving Agents Learn from Privileged Retrospective Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27495) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework where the same model acts as both student and teacher, using privileged retrospective context—cross-task precedents, turn-level reflection, and future hindsight—to distill dense supervision from unlabeled on-policy trajectories. It also proposes frontier-guided context-policy evolution, where a stronger model edits how privileged context is constructed, yielding up to 59.7% improvement over the base model and a further 44.7% relative gain over a fixed context policy on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B. This work addresses a key bottleneck in self-evolving agents: the lack of ground-truth solutions or verifier rewards in naturally collected experience. By converting unlabeled trajectories into dense supervision without external labels, RSD offers a scalable path for agents to improve continuously after deployment, potentially reducing reliance on costly human annotation or reward models. RSD uses the same underlying model as both student and teacher, with the teacher re-scoring the student's realized actions conditioned on privileged retrospective context that includes cross-task precedents, turn-level reflection, and future hindsight from the completed trajectory. The experience bank grows across rounds, refreshing the retrospective context and allowing model, data, and supervision to co-evolve; frontier-guided context-policy evolution further improves results but requires a stronger frontier model.
