## [Bounded rating scales can fabricate effects in LLM-judge difference-in-differences audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27309) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A pre-registered audit of 990 calls to a frozen pedagogy LLM judge shows in closed form that difference-in-differences on a bounded rating scale can produce a spurious interaction when a severity shift common to both responses is attenuated unequally by the scale bounds. The registered primary analysis found no effect of a stated novice versus advanced profile on scaffolding preference, and a post-hoc construction with zero differential preference reproduced 79–85% of the only nominally significant secondary interaction (+0.378 points; p = 0.002) using just the observed severity shift and the scale floor. This is a cautionary methodological result for the fast-growing LLM-as-judge evaluation literature: bias audits and A/B-style comparisons that read interactions off bounded rating scales may certify differential preference that does not exist on the latent scale. Anyone running judge-based bias audits or preference comparisons should check whether scale censoring could explain their interaction before claiming a finding. The paper builds on prior work on nonlinear difference-in-differences and derives the bias in closed form rather than relying on simulation alone; the empirical evidence comes from a pre-registered audit with 990 judge calls plus a post-hoc null simulation. The key caveat is that the result concerns bounded or censored endpoints, so the risk depends on how close ratings sit to the scale floor or ceiling and on whether the common severity shift is large relative to the available range.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-as-judge evaluation uses a capable language model to score or compare outputs, and audits of such judges try to detect bias by contrasting matched conditions. Difference-in-differences is a standard causal-inference design that compares a within-item contrast across a manipulated attribute; here the contrast is between two candidate responses and the outcome is a rating on a bounded scale. When an outcome is bounded, a shift that affects both responses equally can be compressed near the floor or ceiling, and if that compression differs across conditions, the design can register an interaction even when no differential preference exists on the underlying latent scale.

A new arXiv paper (2609.04180) reports that auxiliary views—conceptual reformulations of knowledge—causally improve how large language models learn during pre-training, even for near-verbatim factual recall. Through controlled experiments, the authors show that reallocating tokens from paraphrases to auxiliary views improves learning, and that this benefit does not depend on the strength of the model generating the views. The findings offer a mechanistic explanation for why data diversity matters in pre-training and provide concrete recipes for synthetic data augmentation, which could shape how labs curate pre-training corpora and pursue LLM self-improvement. Researchers and engineers designing training data mixtures for large models are the primary audience. The study finds paraphrasing helps only at smaller batch sizes, identifies knowledge types that aid learning when prior knowledge gaps exist, and analyzes effects mechanistically via layer-wise biases and compression. The results are based on controlled experiments rather than a single large-scale training run, so scaling behavior remains to be validated.

**Background**: Pre-training is the stage where LLMs learn general knowledge from massive text corpora before fine-tuning. Auxiliary views are the web of explanations, analogies, and reformulations humans generate when learning and teaching, as opposed to simple paraphrases that restate the same content. Understanding which data forms drive knowledge acquisition is central to building better training mixtures and synthetic data pipelines.

## [Decentralized Equilibrium Learning Over Dynamic Networks with Logarithmic Regret](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17601) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes networked decentralized optimal equilibrium learning dynamics in which agents exchange time-stamped, time-stacked tables of randomized semantic content/discontent signals rather than raw actions or payoff information, and combines table fusion with temporal majority reconstruction to handle time-varying communication. It establishes finite-time logarithmic regret guarantees, with an in-phase exploration perturbation, for optimal equilibrium selection under utilitarian and proportional-fair social welfare objectives. This work enables multi-agent systems to converge to socially desirable equilibria without a central coordinator, prior knowledge of the game, or high-bandwidth communication, which is important for distributed control, networked markets, and edge multi-agent deployments. The finite-time logarithmic regret guarantee provides a strong theoretical performance bound that is rare in fully decentralized, dynamic-network settings. Agents observe only their own realized payoffs and communicate low-bandwidth randomized semantic signals with time-varying neighbors, so the protocol avoids sharing raw actions, payoffs, or local parameter estimates. The analysis relies on an in-phase exploration perturbation and covers both utilitarian and proportional-fair welfare objectives, with simulation results demonstrating effective equilibrium selection over dynamic networks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: A finite normal-form game models strategic interaction among a fixed number of players, each choosing from a finite set of strategies, and such games always admit a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies. Regret measures the cumulative loss relative to the best fixed strategy in hindsight; logarithmic regret, i.e., growing as O(log T), is a strong guarantee that the learner's average regret vanishes quickly. Social welfare objectives such as utilitarian welfare (sum of utilities) and proportional-fair welfare (which rewards relative improvements across agents) define which equilibrium is considered socially optimal.

EMERGE introduces the first fully SE(3)-equivariant graph-based diffusion backbone for point cloud generation, enabling zero-shot inference at multiple arbitrary spatial resolutions. The resolution-agnostic capability could simplify deployment across applications requiring varying point cloud densities, from robotics to graphics. The framework bypasses the rigid resolution dependencies of standard generative pipelines, allowing zero-shot inference at multiple resolutions without retraining. Strong inherent geometric inductive biases lead to faster training convergence compared to Transformer and VAE-based baselines.

## [OPIS: A New Benchmark for Multi-Object Memory in Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35052) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced OPIS, an input-grounded benchmark with 500 cases and dense object-level annotations for 12,672 rigid, articulated, and deformable instances across real-world, robotic, and game domains, designed to evaluate multi-object memory in video world models. The benchmark includes a hierarchical evaluator measuring Object Presence, Identity, and Structure, and when applied to eight image-to-video or camera-conditioned world models, scores ranged from 48.65 to 56.01. Existing evaluation protocols often rely on generated histories or selected viewpoints that can confound true memory assessment, so OPIS provides a more rigorous, input-anchored standard for measuring whether world models actually preserve specific object instances over time. This matters for video generation and world model research, where consistent object persistence is critical for applications like robotics and interactive simulation. The evaluator combines association and explicit visibility reasoning to hierarchically measure Object Presence, Identity, and Structure, using static or dynamic tracks based on object kinematics. Results show that as the reference inventory grows from fewer than 20 to more than 40 objects, the average Identity score falls from 40.22 to 23.11, highlighting that preserving particular input instances is considerably harder than generating plausible visual elements.

## [UMM-Reflection: Interleaved RL Teaches Unified Models to Self-Repair Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35767) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce UMM-Reflection, which applies trajectory-level reinforcement learning to complete reflection loops inside a single unified multimodal model, so the model can diagnose, revise, and re-render its own images. On BAGEL, it improves GenEval by 12.05 points over supervised fine-tuning, with gains transferring to WISE (+10.97), OneIG-Bench (+3.48), and T2I-CompBench++ (+4.63). This shows that jointly learning reflection text and image rendering over multi-round loops can unlock self-correction gains that neither supervised fine-tuning nor single-head RL achieves, and that these gains generalize to unseen benchmarks. It points toward unified multimodal models that can iteratively fix their own outputs at inference without an external verifier or critic. Sibling reflection trajectories share one initial image, so a group-relative advantage compares different reflection strategies, and a single trajectory-level advantage updates both the reflection tokens and the flow-based image revisions, avoiding combinatorial per-round credit assignment. No verifier is needed at inference, but the abstract is truncated and the approach is evaluated on a single base model (BAGEL).

## [Binarization Flattens the Score Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35797) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.35797v2) shows that collapsing LLM-judge rewards to pass/fail ({0,1}) creates an affine stretch ambiguity: any proportional rescaling of the underlying scores toward or away from the cutoff leaves all verdicts unchanged, so a policy can exploit this without detection. Using a joint-Gaussian model, the authors prove that adding a third grade introduces a second threshold and removes this ambiguity, and they empirically confirm on MATH and SciBench outputs that all 14 constructed criterionwise stretches were invisible after binarization but visible with three grades. This work identifies a concrete blind spot in LLM-as-judge reward modeling used for RLHF and policy training, showing that binary verdicts can mask systematic score distortions that look like genuine improvement. It offers a simple, low-cost fix—retaining at least three grades—that practitioners can adopt to make reward signals more identifiable and harder to game. The paper reports that at n=1,024, a test given both population laws achieved at least 96.5% power under a 1.5× stress, and it notes that the shared-factor reference approximation fit MATH and SciBench but not HealthBench, delineating its empirical scope. It also cautions that verdicts alone remain insufficient: arbitrary within-grade changes and fixed-covariance, loading-aligned mean shifts (a sycophancy-shaped lift the panel reads as competence) are still indistinguishable from genuine improvement, so external validation along the remaining direction is recommended.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-as-judge is a common technique in which a large language model scores or compares outputs, often used as a reward signal in RLHF when deterministic verifiers cannot capture an objective. In many pipelines these judgments are binarized to pass/fail for simplicity, but the paper shows this discards information about how well each criterion was met. MATH and SciBench are benchmarks of competition-level and college-level scientific problems used to evaluate LLM reasoning, making them suitable testbeds for studying judge behavior.

## [BreakingWeb Benchmark Hardens Browser-Use Tasks via Controlled Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35814) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced BreakingWeb, a benchmark of 519 matched task pairs across seven self-hosted websites, where each task is run once on an unmodified site and once under a reproducible, labeled intervention to the site's content, server state, network responses, or rendered page. Evaluating six strong browser-use agents, three screenshot-only agents, and humans, interventions lowered the six agents' pass rates by 22.9 percentage points on average, while humans dropped only 10.0 points on first attempt and 5.7 points on repeat. This work reframes benchmark difficulty as a programmable property of the environment rather than a byproduct of adding new tasks or websites, making it cheaper and more diagnostic to stress-test browser-use agents. It also reveals that most agent failures (75%) are belief failures—agents declaring success without making the required change—which points to a specific reliability gap for web automation in production. Each intervention keeps the user instruction and success criterion fixed, is detectable and workaround-able by a competent user, and is labeled with the behavior recovery mainly requires (e.g., verification); runs are scored against the website's final backend state. The benchmark spans 29 intervention families and seven cognitive primitives, and each agent fails on nearly half of the tasks it solves on the unmodified website.

**Background**: Browser-use agents are AI systems that control a web browser to complete tasks such as filling forms, booking appointments, or retrieving information, and they are typically evaluated on benchmarks of tasks run on live or self-hosted websites. As agents improve, benchmark builders usually add new tasks and sites, which is costly and confounds many variables at once, making it unclear what actually makes a task hard. ## [ROSS selectively supervises historical self-generated rollouts to boost LLM post-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35954) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ROSS introduces selective supervision over preserved historical self-generated rollouts, applying loss only to selected model-generated continuations while keeping the full trajectory as context. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, it raises the six-benchmark MOPD average from 58.40% to 62.20% and SWE-bench Verified from 64.20% to 68.40%. The method shows that self-rollout training leaves behind reusable behavioral experience that can yield further gains through offline supervised fine-tuning without additional policy rollouts, improving performance across reinforcement learning, on-policy distillation, and agentic tasks. This could make post-training more sample-efficient and reduce the cost of generating fresh rollouts. ROSS preserves the full historical trajectory as context but masks the loss so that mistakes, abandoned attempts, and redundant actions are not imitated, and it consistently improves upstream checkpoints across mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and software engineering. The approach is evaluated in domain-specific reinforcement learning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and agentic reinforcement learning settings.

**Background**: Large language model post-training commonly uses reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation, where the model generates its own rollouts and learns from them. These rollouts are usually discarded once the policy updates because they are considered stale, even though they may still contain useful behaviors. On-policy distillation trains a student on its own trajectory distribution, while selective supervision applies loss only to chosen parts of a sequence.

The paper introduces Spectral Null-Space Swap (S³), a training-free method that composes a Non-thinking model's dominant subspace with a Thinking model's null-space component to improve reasoning efficiency. Evaluated on 2B–30B dense and MoE models across 28 environments, S³ reduces inference token overhead by an average of 27.4% while improving accuracy by 1.0 percentage point compared to full Thinking models. It offers a practical, training-free way to cut the token cost of chain-of-thought reasoning, which could make reasoning models cheaper to deploy in latency-sensitive applications. S³ keeps the Non-thinking model inside its own dominant subspace and takes the Thinking checkpoint outside it, and attention entropy analysis shows the retained component yields more concentrated attention. ## [StepRS-GRPO: Stepwise Risk-Sensitive RL for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00661) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces StepRS-GRPO, a reinforcement learning method for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while keeping the underlying GRPO trainer unchanged. Across multiple dLLM backbones and math reasoning benchmarks, it improves pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO and increases answer diversity. This work addresses a key inefficiency in applying RLVR to dLLMs: terminal rewards are reused across parallel denoising decisions even though their conditioning contexts differ. By making credit assignment state-aware without changing the trainer, it offers a lightweight way to improve reasoning and diversity in diffusion-based LLMs, which are an emerging alternative to autoregressive models. For binary rewards, the transformation is shown to be exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages, with a capability-based calibration suggesting the coefficient scale and endpoint/interpolation ablations guiding schedule selection. Ablations with mass-matched controls and RMS-matched advantages support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and reasoning-trace diagnostics show diversity gains extend beyond final-answer strings.

## [FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02198) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FERPO introduces an on-policy maximum-entropy reinforcement learning algorithm that improves policies using critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. It fits the actor to an entropy- and KL-regularized target action distribution via a forward-KL objective estimated with self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). This work addresses a known reliability issue in continuous-control RL: critics trained to predict returns may not provide accurate action gradients, leading to unstable policy updates. By avoiding critic differentiation and using forward KL to encourage coverage of multiple high-value modes, FERPO offers a more stable and exploratory alternative that could benefit sample efficiency in robotics and control tasks. FERPO derives an optimal target action distribution from a policy-improvement objective regularized by entropy and KL divergence, and the KL regularization keeps importance weights well-behaved by limiting deviation from the rollout policy. Experiments on MuJoCo Playground and ManiSkill show competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains, and computational benchmarks demonstrate faster actor updates than Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, popularized by Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), augments the reward with an entropy term to encourage exploration and robustness. Many state-of-the-art continuous-control methods use an actor-critic setup where the actor is updated using gradients of the critic with respect to actions, but critics are trained only to predict returns, so their action gradients can be unreliable. Importance sampling reweights samples from a proposal distribution to estimate expectations under a target distribution, and self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) normalizes the weights for lower variance and stability. Forward and reverse KL divergences behave differently in optimization: reverse KL tends to be mode-seeking, while forward KL encourages covering multiple modes.

## [EDISCO: Equivariant Discrete Diffusion for Euclidean Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04953) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EDISCO is the first discrete diffusion model for Euclidean combinatorial optimization problems (ECOPs) that achieves exact E(2)-invariant generative distributions over node-index solutions, eliminating the need for data augmentation or regularization. It introduces an E(2)-equivariant edge-score network combined with a categorical continuous-time Markov chain over discrete edge variables, and outperforms previous learning-based state-of-the-art solvers on synthetic TSP (100–10000 nodes) and CVRP (50–2000 customers) while using only 33–50% of the training instances. This work addresses a known limitation of learning-based methods for routing problems—approximate symmetry handling—by providing exact equivariance, which could lead to more efficient and robust solvers. It may influence future research in equivariant generative models for combinatorial optimization and logistics. EDISCO's local geometric inductive bias ensures that edge neighborhoods with identical relative geometry and combinatorial context are represented consistently regardless of absolute position or orientation. Trained only on uniform synthetic data, it also outperforms competing learning-based baselines under spatial distribution shift and CVRP constraint-tightness shift, with code available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Euclidean combinatorial optimization problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) involve finding optimal routes and are invariant under rotations, reflections, and translations—the E(2) group. Equivariant neural networks are designed to respect such symmetries by guaranteeing that transformations of the input lead to corresponding transformations of the features, improving generalization. Discrete diffusion models use continuous-time Markov chains to generate discrete structures like edges, offering a principled way to model combinatorial solutions.

## [TAPDreamer: Transferable Adversarial Patches for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06814) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TAPDreamer introduces a fixed adversarial patch that transfers across tasks and action architectures without querying the target policy, using only a public encoder. In closed-loop tests, a single frozen patch covering about 6.5% of the input drops FastWAM's success rate from 97.7% to 0.0% on 40 LIBERO tasks and from 90.86% to 0.0% on 50 RoboTwin tasks. This work shows that world action models, which are foundational for general-purpose robotic control, are vulnerable to persistent local perturbations that corrupt shared visual representations. It implies that defenses must secure the visual encoder itself, not just downstream action generation, affecting AI safety and robotics deployment. The attack exploits interactions between patch-induced attention weight changes and value vectors to broadcast a nearly identical representation shift far beyond the patch footprint, and it uses six frames from one source task to maximize global L1 distance between clean and patched encoder representations. Matched random patches retain 81.5% and 79.2% success, and the same patches reduce success to 1.45% and 1.00% on two DreamWAM configurations and to 10.60% on Motus.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: World models learn to predict how their environment will evolve, and world action models (WAMs) couple future world prediction with executable action generation for robotic control. Adversarial patches are localized image perturbations designed to fool models, and transferability means the patch works on unseen models without access to their parameters. Existing attacks on WAMs optimize against victim outputs and require target-model queries, whereas TAPDreamer avoids this by using a public encoder alone.

## [Delta Distillation Improves Multi-Teacher On-Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10460) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Δ-MOPD, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method that transfers each teacher's teacher-minus-base logit shift re-anchored at the student's frozen initialization, instead of the teacher's endpoint policy. Experiments show that with three composed teachers, Δ-MOPD exceeds endpoint composition by 4.11 Math and 1.95 five-benchmark points, and under phased routing it reduces the order gap from 10.50 to 6.42 points. This work identifies a key mechanism—inherited base pull can exceed the post-training shift—that impedes endpoint transfer in multi-teacher distillation, and offers a simple target-construction fix. It establishes target construction as an independent design axis complementary to teacher selection, which could lead to more effective and stable distillation of multiple specialized capabilities into a single LLM. The method re-anchors each teacher's logit shift at the student's frozen initialization, which reduces the teacher-term norm ratio and target–student KL. Gains are most pronounced when teacher signals are combined at a state (common-domain composition), while under interleaved routing where each update involves one teacher, the two targets perform comparably.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation typically trains a student model to match a teacher's output logits, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends this by using multiple specialized teachers to score student rollouts. However, standard endpoint supervision transfers the teacher's full policy, which mixes what post-training changed with preferences inherited from the teacher's base model. This inherited base pull can dominate the learning signal, making it harder for the student to learn the actual post-training improvements.

## [CRISP: Pixel-Space Diffusion Decoder Eliminates Flying Pixels in LiDAR Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11376) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CRISP introduces a pixel-space diffusion decoder that replaces latent decoders in LiDAR generation pipelines, significantly reducing flying pixel artifacts and improving metrics across KITTI-360, SemanticKITTI, and nuScenes. The decoder alone reduces FSVD/FPVD by 50.5% on average across frozen backbones, with reductions reaching 71%/74% for generic video VAEs and a 71% drop in FRID on the LiDAR-native LiDM backbone. Flying pixels are a major bottleneck in latent LiDAR generation, causing unrealistic point clouds that hinder downstream perception and simulation. CRISP's backbone-agnostic decoder replacement offers a simple, effective fix that could improve the realism of generated LiDAR data for autonomous driving, benefiting researchers and practitioners using generative models for 3D scene synthesis. CRISP uses a backbone-agnostic latent adapter, a DiT-based denoiser, and a support mask predictor, and can be applied zero-shot to pretrained models like LiDM, improving FSVD by 15.5% and narrowing the sim-to-real gap. The largest gains occur at depth discontinuities, and code and checkpoints will be released.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Latent LiDAR generation pipelines typically encode point clouds into a latent space using a convolutional VAE, generate new latents with a diffusion model, and decode them back to point clouds. Convolutional VAE decoders tend to blur sharp depth discontinuities, producing 'flying pixels'—points that float between surfaces after back-projection. Diffusion transformers (DiTs) are transformer-based denoisers that have become standard in image and video generation, offering an alternative to convolutional U-Nets.

## [StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Models with RL for Calibrated Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17309) ⭐️ 7.0/10

StartLux-Decision introduces decision models ranging from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine single-pass prediction with confidence-guided adaptive reasoning, and a new reinforcement learning method called RLCD^2 that rewards calibrated decision probabilities while penalizing overly long reasoning traces. The 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4 on the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, and AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy on the new DecisionPivot benchmark. This work addresses a key tension in deploying language models for decisions: reasoning improves accuracy but is slow and costly, while single-pass prediction is fast but poorly calibrated. By using confidence to decide when to reason and by directly optimizing calibration with RLCD^2, the approach could make deliberative decision models more practical for real-world applications where both reliability and latency matter. RLCD^2 uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality, and it raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points while cutting average reasoning length by up to 65%, largely preserving accuracy. The models can be run with frameworks such as vLLM and MLX, and quantized versions are available to reduce memory usage.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Calibration refers to how well a model's predicted probabilities match actual outcomes; a well-calibrated model that says it is 80% confident should be correct about 80% of the time. Proper scoring rules are mathematical functions used to evaluate and reward calibrated probabilistic predictions, and they form the basis of the RLCD^2 reward. Adaptive reasoning means a model can choose to invoke explicit chain-of-thought only for uncertain cases, saving compute on confident ones.

## [Linearly Decodable Facts Generalize Better After Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22300) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22300v2) introduces a distinction between 'active' facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, and 'inert' facts, which can be recalled but do not generalize. Across 11 language models and 70 relations, the linear readability of the original relation in pretrained representations strongly predicts generalization to held-out subjects after fine-tuning, with Pearson correlations of 0.87 to 0.92 within each model. This work offers mechanistic insight into why some knowledge generalizes after fine-tuning while other knowledge remains inert, which could inform data selection and fine-tuning strategies for LLMs. It also bridges mechanistic interpretability (linear probing) with practical fine-tuning outcomes, relevant to AI/ML researchers and practitioners. The association persists when controlling for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and subject frequency in pretraining text, and is robust to re-randomizing label assignments and fine-tuning seeds. When mapping wrong labels back to original answers, recovered answers are more often among the linear probe's top answers than the pretrained model's own, suggesting the probe captures task-relevant structure.

## [CCR packs three problems per rollout to cut RLVR token costs by ~80%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22887) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR), which packs three independently verifiable problems into one capped training completion, and shows that on 4B and 8B math reasoning models it reduces tokens per training step from 975,464 to 174,957 (82.1% saving) and from 793,832 to 165,788 (79.1% saving), respectively, compared with single-problem GRPO using a 32k window. Long rollout windows are a major cost driver in RLVR, and CCR shows that reward-preserving training structure can cut per-step cost by roughly 5.6x without simply truncating away the correctness signal, which matters for anyone training reasoning models under tight compute budgets. Correct answers completed before truncation retain credit, while a shared budget encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty; the authors connect this mechanism to conditional reward- and update-variance analyses, and an 8B training trace shows increasing accuracy reward alongside shorter completions, with single-problem evaluations supporting retained reasoning quality.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) fine-tunes LLMs using automatic rule-based checkers instead of learned reward models, and GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a popular critic-free RL algorithm that normalizes rewards within a group of completions to the same prompt. In GRPO, if every rollout for a problem truncates before producing an answer, all rewards in the group are identical and the relative advantage vanishes, removing the learning signal. This paper is a technical continuation of Batched Contextual Reinforcement (BCR) and studies how concurrent rewards relax the need for long rollout windows.

## [MoEvolve: Bidirectional Distillation Strengthens MoE LLMs via Internal Teacher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23185) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework that first expands the activation budget (top-k) of a Mixture-of-Experts LLM to create a stronger internal teacher, then reverses distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-k model. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to 22.2 domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to 6.5 points. This work addresses a key limitation of RLVR—sparse outcome-level rewards—by leveraging the MoE architecture itself to provide dense token-level supervision without needing an external stronger teacher. It offers a practical, self-contained post-training method that could make MoE models more capable without increasing inference-time activation budgets. Naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together; MoEvolve therefore follows a recovery-then-improvement strategy, first restoring the high-k model and then strengthening it before reversing distillation. Notably, the final low-k models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers, and the method retains the original inference-time activation budget.

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs use a top-k routing mechanism to activate only a subset of experts per token, keeping inference efficient. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves such models using automatic, rule-based rewards, but provides only sparse outcome-level supervision. On-policy distillation offers dense token-level feedback but typically requires a stronger compatible teacher model, which may not be available.

## [HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24452) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HumanSkill-4D introduces a training-free framework for avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries and can also specify poses or motions to select matching intervals. It addresses region and motion ambiguity by sharing a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars, using a semantic memory and a motion memory to make selections traceable. This work enables natural-language interaction with animatable 3D avatars for local editing and motion inspection, which could simplify workflows in virtual production, gaming, and telepresence. It also introduces three human-annotated benchmarks for avatar referring segmentation, filling a gap in evaluation for language grounding in 4D avatar representations. The framework requires only minutes of setup per avatar and uses compact memories, with the MLLM composing operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories. It outperforms baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, though the approach is evaluated on human-annotated benchmarks and may depend on the quality of the underlying Gaussian avatar representation.

## [FALCON: Counterexample-Grounded Verification for Secure Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25916) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce FALCON, a counterexample-grounded verification framework that separates attack exploration from behavioral verification by linking them through execution traces of the program under test. In test-time repair and as an RL reward, FALCON yields substantially stronger held-out functional-security gains than alternative security signals across secure code generation benchmarks. Reliable security verification is becoming a central bottleneck as coding models and agent harnesses grow more capable, and FALCON addresses the risk that optimizers improve a security signal's verdict without removing the underlying vulnerability. This work could improve the trustworthiness of agentic coding systems and mitigate reward overoptimization in security-focused RL. FALCON connects attack exploration and behavioral verification via execution traces, avoiding the need for models to infer program behavior from source code or specify correct outcomes for adversarial tests. Combining FALCON with proxy rewards further improves held-out performance, suggesting execution-grounded feedback can preserve useful guidance from existing security signals while reducing overoptimization.

Counterexample-grounded verification uses concrete failing inputs (counterexamples) to guide the search for vulnerabilities and validate fixes.

## [TamedFlow: Trajectory-Aware Distillation for Teacher-Assisted Diffusion Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26025) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TamedFlow introduces a trajectory-aware distillation method that trains a compressed Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to remain robust when combined with adaptive inference, addressing a failure mode called the 'Combination Gap'. The approach uses cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision, achieving FID 2.58 at 2.25× speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256×256 when distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2. This work identifies and addresses a concrete failure mode that arises when two popular acceleration strategies—model compression and adaptive inference—are combined, which is increasingly relevant as practitioners seek to deploy diffusion models efficiently. The proposed solution could enable more reliable and faster generative modeling in resource-constrained settings, impacting areas like image and video generation. The method includes a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator (LTE) that routes completed drafts at inference: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Ablations show that trajectory supervision is beneficial and that LTE routing outperforms random decisions at nearly matched latency; evaluations extend to ImageNet 512×512, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics.

A new arXiv paper (2610.26443v2) proposes WSR-Tune, a fine-tuning framework that constructs a safety-conditioned basis to reparameterize LLM weight matrices, concentrating safety-relevant information into a small subset of directions. These safety-critical directions are then frozen during downstream adaptation, while the remaining complementary directions are updated, aiming to reduce interference between safety and task objectives. Fine-tuning LLMs on downstream tasks often erodes their safety alignment, creating a trade-off between task performance and safety. WSR-Tune offers a parameter-space structuring approach that could enable safer deployment of adapted models without sacrificing downstream accuracy, which is important for enterprises and researchers who need to customize LLMs while maintaining guardrails. The method explicitly disentangles safety and task information by freezing safety-critical directions in the reparameterized space, and experiments show a more favorable trade-off between downstream performance and safety retention. However, the abstract is truncated, so details on the safety-conditioned basis construction, evaluation benchmarks, and potential limitations are not fully available.

Prior work has tried to identify safety-relevant neurons, layers, or update directions in the original parameter space, but safety information is often distributed across many directions, making it vulnerable to being overwritten. Weight space reparameterization, like weight normalization, is a known technique that transforms weights to improve optimization; WSR-Tune adapts this idea to isolate safety-relevant subspaces.

It also enables modular continual adaptation, where new adapters can be added or updated without touching the backbone or other adapters, which could simplify maintenance and scaling of agent systems. The approach keeps the backbone frozen and exposes adapter selection as an internal action through tool calling, allowing on-demand capability composition in a shared context. ## [Learned Control Variates Speed Up Rare Grid-Outage Estimation for EV Charging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27159) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes a control variate (CV) method that uses a learned classifier of feeder overload, trained on cheap features like temperature and load forecasts, to reduce the number of expensive grid simulations needed for rare-event probability estimation. The authors prove that variance reduction is an explicit function of the classifier's recall and false-positive rate, and show empirically that a boosted-tree learner removes about 60% of the variance, while a single-feature weak learner removes a quarter. Planners need to estimate extremely small outage probabilities to design reliable distribution grids, but plain Monte Carlo with expensive simulators is often prohibitively slow. The theoretical analysis shows that a CV based on a Gaussian proxy of load loses its effectiveness as outages become rarer, whereas a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. Numerical experiments span three orders of magnitude of outage probability, and the Surabaya case shows the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27398) proves that the closed-form bounds for probabilities of causation (PoCs) proposed by Shu et al. for multi-valued treatments and outcomes are sharp in arbitrary dimensions, closing a previously open problem. It further shows that PNS, PSub, PRep, and PN are all special cases of a single general formula, yielding a unified theorem for sharp bounds on discrete PoCs from experimental and observational data. This settles the theoretical question of sharp bounds for discrete probabilities of causation in every dimension, which matters for applications such as personalized medicine, marketing, and legal attribution where causal responsibility must be quantified from data. It also unifies previously separate causal measures under one formula, simplifying both theory and future practical estimation. The proof is purely mathematical and builds on the validity result of Shu et al., extending sharpness from low dimensions to arbitrary dimensions. The unification covers PNS, PSub, PRep, and PN together with their equivalence classes, so that a single theorem gives closed-form sharp bounds for all discrete PoCs.

This empirical result challenges the common practitioner assumption that dividing review work among multiple LLM agents automatically improves reliability, showing that gains in recall come at the cost of more false alarms and much higher token usage. ## [AnomalyAgent: Agentic Ensemble of Vision-Language Models for Visual Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28560) ⭐️ 6.0/10

AnomalyAgent is a post-training fusion framework that uses a constrained vision-language model to select score and map fusion actions for combining heterogeneous pretrained anomaly detectors. It explicitly handles detector disagreement by summarizing score- and region-level conflicts and treating fusion as a finite action-selection problem. Most existing ensembles rely on fixed fusion rules that fail when pretrained detectors disagree, so an adaptive, agentic fusion approach could improve robustness in industrial visual anomaly detection where labeled anomalies are scarce. It also illustrates a broader trend of using vision-language models as decision-making agents inside computer vision pipelines. The framework defines score actions (consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, score-map consistency) and map actions (consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, disagreement correction), with the VLM only invoked on high-conflict samples. It is evaluated on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks, plus seven additional public anomaly benchmarks and Real-IAD for large-scale score-level evaluation, reporting the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among compared fusion methods.

The paper introduces CA-MOPD, a method that first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher-student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Across six benchmarks, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. By dynamically adjusting supervision based on estimated capability gaps, CA-MOPD offers a more efficient and effective way to integrate multiple specialized teachers into a single student model, potentially improving LLM post-training pipelines. CA-MOPD decreases supervision as capability gaps close and increases it when student capability regresses, while teachers still provide dense token-level guidance. The method is evaluated on six benchmarks covering mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, with controlled comparisons supporting the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.

By balancing these two signals, DDCI achieves more stable and narrower prediction intervals while maintaining near-nominal coverage. This work addresses a key limitation of existing online conformal methods for time series, which rely solely on miscoverage indicators and can produce overly wide or unstable intervals. DDCI's dual-feedback mechanism could lead to more efficient and reliable uncertainty quantification in sequential forecasting applications such as finance, energy, and healthcare. DDCI uses actual feedback to drive primary interval adjustments based on true observations, while estimated feedback from an oracle conformal method dampens excessive expansions or contractions during updates. The method maintains near-nominal coverage in practice, though theoretical guarantees and comparisons to other online conformal methods are not detailed in the abstract.

**Background**: Conformal prediction is a distribution-free uncertainty quantification framework that produces prediction sets or intervals with guaranteed coverage under exchangeability. For time series, temporal dependence and distribution shifts violate exchangeability, so online conformal methods adaptively adjust prediction thresholds using feedback from past errors. Recent advances use miscoverage indicators to update intervals, but they ignore the empirical threshold from an oracle conformal method that could provide additional stability.

## [CoASFL: Tackling Coupled Inconsistencies in Asynchronous Split Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26992) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CoASFL introduces an inconsistency-aware asynchronous split federated learning framework that mitigates horizontal inconsistency across clients and vertical inconsistency between clients and the server through dynamic activation merging and consistency-aware model aggregation. Experiments on an 80-device heterogeneous edge testbed show 1.61× to 3.74× training speedup and up to 3.26% higher final accuracy compared to state-of-the-art SFL approaches. Asynchronous split federated learning is critical for training large models on resource-constrained edge devices, but the coupled inconsistencies it introduces can cause model divergence and client drift. CoASFL's joint coordination of activation-level and model-level consistency offers a practical path to more stable and efficient asynchronous training in heterogeneous edge environments. The framework constructs more consistent activation sequences from heterogeneous clients to alleviate horizontal inconsistency, and dynamically adjusts aggregation weights based on client participation frequencies and progress gaps to mitigate vertical inconsistency. The evaluation uses an 80-device heterogeneous edge testbed, though the paper does not specify the model architectures or datasets used.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Split federated learning (SFL) combines federated learning's privacy-preserving distributed training with split learning's model-splitting approach, where a model is divided between resource-constrained clients and a server. Asynchronous SFL allows the server to aggregate without waiting for slow clients (stragglers), but this introduces temporal inconsistencies: clients may be at different training stages (horizontal inconsistency) and client-server model parts may be out of sync (vertical inconsistency). These issues are worsened by non-IID data across clients, which causes client drift—where local updates diverge from the global objective.

Ablation and interpretability analyses support the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components, and case studies show early enrichment of bioactive compounds.

BR-MoE proposes a budgeted semantic release framework that extends a published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts pipeline for traffic scene description. It uses four scene experts, an RL controller that allocates privacy budget per release, and calibrated noise before text conversion, claiming an event-level differential privacy bound under chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions. ## [BMO: Boundary-Aware Model Obfuscation Defends Edge Models Against Cross-Node Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27135) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes BMO, a boundary-aware model obfuscation method that decomposes model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components using null-space constraints, then injects noise into the curvature component to diversify decision boundaries. Across four adversarial attack types and four on-device models, BMO achieves an average defense success rate of 68.68%, far exceeding the best baseline's 22.32%, while maintaining comparable benign accuracy. This work addresses a critical security risk in on-device machine learning: when one edge device is compromised, attackers can obtain white-box access to the deployed model and potentially endanger all models distributed from the same source. BMO offers a defense that significantly improves robustness against cross-node attacks without sacrificing benign performance, which could be valuable for privacy-sensitive edge deployments. BMO is evaluated against four major types of adversarial attacks on four widely-deployed on-device models, showing an average defense success rate of 68.68% versus 22.32% for the most competitive baseline. The method preserves benign accuracy comparable to baselines, but as an arXiv preprint it has not yet undergone peer review and the abstract is truncated, limiting full assessment.

## [ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27142) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ICLHerd introduces a herding-based data selection framework that uses a von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking and mode-averaging, addressing the mode-seeking bias of existing max-similarity methods. It also proposes in-context learning as a validation proxy to enable efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Data selection is critical for LLM training quality, and ICLHerd's approach could improve downstream performance by selecting more diverse and representative training data. The use of in-context learning as a proxy also offers a cheaper alternative to full fine-tuning for hyperparameter validation, potentially making data selection more practical for large-scale training. The method replaces cosine similarity with a von Mises-Fisher kernel, which is a directional distribution on the sphere, to interpolate between mode-seeking and mode-averaging behavior. The balance hyperparameter is tuned via in-context learning performance, avoiding expensive model retraining for each candidate setting.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: In LLM training, data selection often involves curating a development set that represents desired skills and then selecting training samples similar to it, typically using cosine distance over hidden states or gradients. However, this max-similarity strategy tends to pick data that cluster tightly around the development samples, leading to a mode-seeking bias that reduces diversity. Herding algorithms are a family of methods that select samples to match the distribution of a target set, and the von Mises-Fisher distribution is a probability distribution for directional data on a sphere. In-context learning allows a model to perform tasks by conditioning on examples without parameter updates, making it a lightweight validation signal.

## [Linguistic Similarity Predicts Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27285) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A large-scale study across 14 languages finds that linguistic similarity is the strongest predictor of cross-lingual hate speech detection transfer, with temporal overlap and dataset-size difference playing smaller roles. The authors also hypothesize that shared cultural cues and communicative norms may explain residual patterns, though this is presented as a qualitative observation rather than a measured cause. This work provides practical guidance for when cross-lingual transfer can support hate-speech detection in low-resource languages and where its limitations emerge, informing the design of more reliable multilingual moderation systems. It also highlights that measurable linguistic factors do not fully explain transfer patterns, pointing to cultural context as a promising direction for future research. The study covers 14 languages including low-resource ones, and finds consistent patterns where certain language pairs transfer more effectively than others. The cultural interpretation is explicitly framed as a hypothesis from qualitative inspection rather than a measured cause, and the authors note that measurable factors do not fully explain the observed patterns.

## [Trail-Weighted Pruning of Evidence for Bayesian Network Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27366) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces trail-weighted pruning of evidence for approximate outcome prediction in Bayesian networks, where a traversal scores each active trail by the product of its edge strengths and drops evidence below a threshold. It proves error bounds for collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables and shows in simulations on random trees that thresholding trail scores yields 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. This work provides a theoretically grounded pruning criterion for approximate inference in Bayesian networks, which could help scale predictions when exact inference is costly. It also offers a computable error bound for simple network structures, advancing understanding of when evidence can be safely discarded. The bound holds only when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node and fails when dropped trails share a branch; for general networks with colliders and loops, the score is applied as an unproven heuristic. On seven bnlearn networks, keeping the top half of evidence by trail score beat random pruning but was not clearly better than mutual-information ranking, and scoring cost more than the inference it saved on six of seven networks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Bayesian networks are probabilistic graphical models that represent conditional dependencies among variables via a directed acyclic graph, and exact inference can be expensive in large networks. Active trails are paths in the graph that carry probabilistic influence between nodes, and pruning evidence means ignoring some observed variables to speed up prediction. Colliders are nodes where two arrows meet head-to-head, which block or activate trails depending on observed evidence.

## [CVG-SGM Memory Recovers Object Identities Across Visibility Gaps in 4D Scene Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27505) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduce CVG-SGM, a transfer-maintain-read memory mechanism that recovers object identities when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and reappears as a new detection. In a controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, it achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy versus 0.570 for no-memory and no-write controls, and correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections on real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes. Persistent object identity is essential for 4D scene graphs to support reliable long-term reasoning in dynamic environments, and this work shows that relational history alone can bridge visibility gaps when appearance and motion cues are unavailable. The approach could improve perception frontends for robotics and autonomous systems that must track objects through occlusion or containment. The method uses geometry-weighted cross-node interaction to transfer target evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU to maintain it during transport, and a two-time readout combining stored carrier-identity compatibility with current detection-carrier geometry. However, it remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.

The paper proposes a framework for unsupervised adaptation of pretrained vision-language models (PVLMs) that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. It constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, while cascaded consistency learning uses temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views. Unsupervised adaptation is crucial for deploying PVLMs in real-world scenarios where target-domain labels are unavailable and domain shift degrades zero-shot performance. This lightweight approach, which updates only normalization parameters and class prototypes, offers a practical way to improve target-domain accuracy without labeled validation data, potentially benefiting applications in medical imaging, autonomous driving, and other fields with distribution shifts. The framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts to preserve pretrained embedding structure. Experiments with CLIP and SigLIP backbones across multiple recognition benchmarks show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods.

## [AnchorRM: Parallel Intra-Batch State Reconstruction for Temporal GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27558) ⭐️ 6.0/10

AnchorRM introduces an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states in memory-based temporal graph neural networks without sequential recurrent updates. It treats the last committed node memory as a fixed pre-batch anchor and predicts residuals from causally preceding same-batch interactions, enabling parallel computation within the batch. This addresses the known trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity in temporal mini-batching, where later interactions in a batch use stale pre-batch memory. The method achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x) across four datasets and three backbones, potentially improving scalability of memory-based temporal graph learning. The reconstructed states are computed in parallel because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, preserving temporal causality. Experiments show competitive predictive performance, but the abstract is truncated, limiting assessment of empirical impact and potential limitations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGNs) maintain recurrent node memories, often updated via GRUs, to capture evolving interaction histories. Temporal mini-batching processes multiple events together for efficiency, but when a node appears multiple times in a batch, later events use stale pre-batch memory because intermediate updates are not yet committed. This problem worsens with larger batch sizes, creating a trade-off between efficiency and temporal fidelity.

## [TRCM: Topology-Aware Route-Consistency Modeling for Neural CVRP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27568) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TRCM introduces a topology-aware route-consistency modeling approach that explicitly predicts pairwise same-route probabilities to guide autoregressive node selection for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). Under matched decoding budgets, it reduces the optimality gap from 3.67% to 3.28% on CVRP50 and from 2.11% to 1.99% on CVRP100, and with 8-fold augmented inference it further lowers the CVRP100 gap from 1.61% to 1.49%. This work shows that explicitly modeling route-level customer co-assignment can improve autoregressive neural solvers for CVRP, a core logistics optimization problem, without changing the underlying construction pipeline. It suggests a practical structural principle that could be integrated into existing neural combinatorial optimization models to gain accuracy at modest cost. Because same-route supervision is class-imbalanced and structurally uneven, TRCM combines structure-preserving augmentation with Topological Entropy (TE)-based reweighting to emphasize locally ambiguous customer pairs. On XML100, TRCM with 8-fold augmentation improves the average objective by 0.24%, and a controlled demand-reassignment test over 500 variants shows more concentrated objective fluctuations.

At very low temperatures, the learned realization is markedly more robust than the training-free variants.

## [VLA-Retain benchmarks cross-dimension robustness effects of vision tuning in VLA models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27698) ⭐️ 6.0/10

VLA-Retain introduces a benchmark that compares five open vision-language-action (VLA) models fine-tuned on camera-view or sensor-noise data against their base checkpoints across seven perturbation dimensions on the LIBERO-Plus dataset. The study finds that targeted vision tuning is not local: mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model-domain configurations, with X-VLA gaining 69.4 percentage points on the target but losing 4.6 points elsewhere, while OpenVLA-OFT gains 39.3 and 1.4 points respectively. This work highlights that success on the target domain alone is insufficient for VLA adaptation, and that cross-dimensional retention should be a key criterion when fine-tuning visual modules for robot manipulation. It affects robotics and VLA researchers who rely on targeted fine-tuning to improve robustness, showing that such tuning can cause regressions on other perturbation dimensions. The benchmark separates target gains from off-target changes, isolates adaptation effects from architectural differences, and rules out generic forgetting by comparing against base checkpoints. It also finds that broader training coverage raises overall gain but does not eliminate dimension-level regressions, and that tuning strategies are model-dependent: DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain to +1.2 points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's to -23.1.

The paper introduces a per-coordinate cap on the ℓ1 perturbation budget, enforced via exact in-loop projection, and evaluates it on APGD-ℓ1, SLIDE, and FMN-ℓ1 attacks. ## [SMART: Segment-Level Rubric Framework for Semantic ASR Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27820) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SMART introduces a segment-level, context-aware rubric-based framework that maps reference-hypothesis discrepancies into coherent segments and assigns explicit consequence labels, enabling traceable semantic evaluation of ASR transcripts. It achieves 0.843 F1 against majority-vote human labels, outperforming direct LLM judgment (0.745 F1), and defines Semantic Impact Error Rate (SIER) to quantify consequential errors at utterance, chunk, and lexical levels. Traditional WER treats all lexical edits equally, ignoring semantic consequences, while overall semantic scores cannot pinpoint which errors alter meaning. SMART addresses this gap by providing fine-grained, traceable error assessment that could improve ASR correction and evaluation, benefiting ASR researchers and practitioners who need to understand the real impact of recognition errors. SMART is relatively insensitive to the choice of evaluation LLM, and its SIER metric reveals different aspects of ASR quality compared to MER. A separate target-reference-free rubric guides correction using the target hypothesis and surrounding ASR hypotheses, outperforming a matched baseline with absolute reductions of 0.85–0.98 percentage points in MER and 1.18–1.65 percentage points in SIER_lex.

## [PULSE: Selective Peer Collaboration for Personalized Learning on Wearables](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28081) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose PULSE, an event-driven framework for personalized opportunistic learning on wearable devices that treats each encounter with a nearby peer as an online decision, incorporating peer gradients only when they are compatible with the local learning direction. Across human activity recognition, fall detection, and stress recognition tasks, PULSE preserved or improved personalized classification performance while reducing peer-assisted exchanges by 80–94% compared with opportunistic model averaging. This work addresses a key tension in on-device personalization: purely local adaptation is limited by scarce data on a single wearable, while conventional federated learning assumes stable connectivity that wearables rarely have. By making peer collaboration selective and cheap, PULSE points toward practical post-deployment personalization for health and well-being applications on resource-constrained hardware. The framework was evaluated under both synthetic and real contact traces, and on-device experiments showed that peer-assisted operations require limited energy, with the complete implementation occupying 149.8 KiB of RAM and 561.8 KiB of flash. The approach also uses past interactions to guide future peer selection, adding a lightweight memory component to the decision process.

The paper introduces BAIT (Bias Annotation In Text), a benchmark consisting of a nine-trigger schema and 50 English news articles annotated at the article and span levels by trained annotators, to evaluate whether LLMs can detect and locate cognitive bias triggers. It benchmarks six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three or ten in-context examples, finding that models approach human agreement on which triggers an article contains but rarely recover the full set and reach less than half of human agreement in locating the spans that carry them. As LLMs increasingly mediate how people encounter news by summarizing, ranking, and answering questions over it, their ability to recognize manipulative language is critical for media literacy and LLM safety. The finding that models respond to surface cues rather than the mechanisms that make a passage manipulative suggests current evaluation and mitigation strategies may be insufficient. The dataset is small (50 articles) and the abstract is truncated, limiting assessment of impact; the models over-predict triggers with easy surface cues, and most passages they mark for these triggers are not actual triggers yet carry the trigger's surface cue far more often than random text. The authors release the schema, codebook, standoff annotations, and evaluation pipeline.

## [TEPCA co-aligns LLM evidence and parameters for temporal knowledge graph reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28176) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces TEPCA, a framework that co-aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it uses time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning and Mutual-Information-based pruning; at the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism. Experiments on two TKG benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, and DG-LoRA is further evaluated on eight commonsense QA datasets. LLMs often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with dynamic real-world knowledge, and existing RAG and PEFT methods are insufficient for temporal reasoning. TEPCA addresses this gap by jointly improving evidence retrieval and parameter adaptation, which could benefit applications requiring time-sensitive reasoning over evolving knowledge graphs. The DRGP pruning preserves globally coherent temporal paths, while MI-based pruning retains query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. DG-LoRA dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context, enabling fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency.

## [CALM: Offline-Calibrated Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28192) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduce CALM (Calibrated Allocation for Layer-Head Merging), which uses offline calibration to assign non-uniform token-merging ratios across attention layers and heads in autoregressive video generation. Experiments on three autoregressive video models show CALM reduces LPIPS to original videos by about 21% versus uniform token merging under the same memory budget, while also achieving higher video-quality scores. KV-cache memory growth is a major bottleneck for streaming long-video generation, and this work shows that a one-time offline calibration can make online compression substantially more effective without retraining. The finding that layer-head sensitivity patterns are consistent across prompts suggests a reusable, model-specific risk map that could be adopted by other efficient-inference pipelines. Because exhaustively evaluating all layer-head allocations is prohibitively expensive, CALM uses attention-output error as a lightweight proxy that strongly correlates with end-to-end video quality, builds a fixed layer-head risk map offline, and then applies dynamic programming at inference time to allocate merging ratios under a given cache budget. The approach is training-free and evaluated across three autoregressive video models, though the calibration is model-specific and must be redone for new architectures.

**Background**: Autoregressive video generation models produce video frame by frame in a streaming fashion, and each new frame attends to cached keys and values (the KV cache) from previous frames, causing memory to grow rapidly with video length. Token merging reduces this cost by clustering temporally redundant tokens and keeping only a few representatives, but prior methods apply the same merging ratio to every attention layer and head. CALM instead exploits the observation that different layers and heads have different, yet stable, sensitivities to merging.

## [Adaptive Pullback OPD: Reweighting Supervision at Penalty Jumps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28194) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper identifies 'penalty jumps' in on-policy distillation (OPD) where average token penalty abruptly rises while teacher confidence drops, a pattern termed penalty-confidence tension, and proposes Adaptive Pullback OPD (AP-OPD) to reweight supervision at these boundaries. AP-OPD uses the preceding block as a local reference and uniformly scales supervision coefficients in the following block so that its weighted average penalty matches the preceding block's original mean, improving performance on mathematical reasoning and code generation. This work introduces a novel diagnostic for OPD training dynamics and a targeted reweighting method that could improve stability and performance of LLM post-training, particularly for reasoning and coding tasks. It highlights the importance of local changes in supervision signals beyond aggregate penalty values, offering a practical technique for practitioners using on-policy distillation. The method detects jumps by comparing consecutive blocks of tokens within the same response, and the scaling factor is determined by the local reference without an additional strength constant. However, the approach is validated only on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, and its effectiveness at larger scale remains to be tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training technique where a student model learns from token-level supervision provided by a stronger teacher on the student's own generated responses. The supervision is based on the log-ratio of student and teacher probabilities for each token, with positive log-ratios penalizing tokens that the student assigns higher probability than the teacher. OPD combines the on-policy relevance of reinforcement learning with the dense reward signal of distillation, and is widely used for LLM post-training.

## [TPO: Tri-level Distributionally Robust Learning for OOD Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28229) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TPO introduces a tri-level distributionally robust learning framework for out-of-distribution direct preference optimization (DPO) that jointly models group-, prompt-, and preference-level distribution shifts. It uses a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set instantiated with Wasserstein distance to derive a tractable objective combining a closed-form preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each with an independent radius. This work addresses a critical gap in robust DPO methods by explicitly modeling the hierarchical structure of out-of-distribution preference shifts, which is essential for safe LLM deployment in real-world scenarios where training and deployment distributions differ. It provides finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirical validation, offering a more principled approach to alignment under distribution shift. The method instantiates the ambiguity set with Wasserstein distance, yielding a tractable and interpretable objective with three independently tuned radii for preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial perturbation, and group reweighting. The paper establishes finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically compares TPO against existing robust DPO methods.

**Background**: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a popular method for aligning large language models with human preferences by directly optimizing a policy on pairwise preference comparisons, but it assumes that the training preference distribution matches the deployment distribution. Identification relies on sufficient variability across domains and uses only second-order statistics, avoiding parametric dependency assumptions or interventions. The method requires multiple domains with differing scalings and was validated on simulated data and an fMRI dataset, but its performance may degrade if domain variability is insufficient.

A new arXiv paper analyzes 16,575 English tweets and introduces a metric called 'stability delta' to show that emojis used in topically coherent contexts have more polarized sentiment, not less. The central correlation is Spearman ρ = +0.361 (Holm p = 0.015) against the Kralj Novak et al. (2015) lexicon, and ρ = +0.509 (p = 0.0003) against Ferré et al. (2025) Spanish emotion ratings. The result survives permutation testing, BCa bootstrap, leave-one-out jackknife, partial correlation controlling for emoji frequency, and Holm correction across a four-test family. A downstream sarcasm classification check on the Emoji Sarcasm Dataset shows all three baselines exceed 0.97 macro F1, indicating saturating emoji-label cues, and the authors frame the classifier as supporting evidence rather than the main contribution.

Researchers introduced DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. Evaluating five vision-language trackers (VLTs) on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching, they found that only Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use, while UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics. Model-internal analyses show that correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable at decision-near states in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems, with decodability peaking at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change. However, because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, the interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue.

TaskWAM is evaluated on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, showing reduced confusion and competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. An integrative review of 72 references proposes five conditions of collective learning capacity—recognizing and retaining knowledge, transmitting it across institutions, protecting consequential challenge, authorizing correction, and preserving feasible alternatives—along with concepts like authoritative corrigibility and retained option value to explain how institutions can maintain accountable, revisable AI sovereignty. It compares the US, China, and France and introduces Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) to organize OECD, IMF, and World Bank indicators around information resources, absorption, and institutional coordination. This work shifts the AI sovereignty debate from resource control to institutional learning and correction, offering a conceptual framework for policymakers and governance scholars to assess whether nations can adapt and remain accountable. It highlights that formal arrangements and resources do not guarantee corrective outcomes, which is crucial as AI systems become more pervasive and consequential. The review uses six reading dimensions (subject, object, scale, mechanism, legitimacy, evidence) and notes that HCLM's national-level parameters are not estimated; conclusions are constrained by purposeful source selection, uneven case coverage, and aggregate measurement. The indicators show different resource profiles and trajectories but leave the operation of correction and feasible exit largely unmeasured.
