A new arXiv paper introduces Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), a Bayesian hierarchical method that estimates full software-agent benchmark scores from a small task subset by combining source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. On four SWE-bench-family task banks at a 10% budget, HSPR achieved the lowest mean absolute error on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error on all four compared to baseline methods. HSPR's use of posterior-guided task selection and hierarchical modeling offers a principled alternative to simple subset averaging, which may be valuable for researchers and practitioners who need reliable agent rankings under budget constraints. HSPR's score-based acquisition criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance, and the final estimate uses the posterior median with source-selected calibration. Evaluating deep generative models for fidelity, diversity, and novelty remains a persistent challenge, and FLD is a theoretically grounded but computationally expensive metric. DRAPE introduces a prompt-learning framework that generates instance-specific soft prompts for multimodal continual instruction tuning (MCIT) by deriving prompt queries from the textual instruction and cross-attending to visual patch features, rather than selecting from a fixed pool of task-level prompts. It mitigates forgetting via null-space gradient projection on the shared projector and uses CLIP-based prototype routing for task-label-free generator selection at inference. This work shifts MCIT from task-level module routing to instance-level adaptation, potentially improving performance on diverse samples within the same task and offering a more granular approach to continual learning for multimodal LLMs. It could influence future research on prompt-based continual learning and deployment of MLLMs in dynamic real-world settings. DRAPE prepends generated prompts to a frozen LLM, uses null-space gradient projection to protect shared parameters, and employs CLIP-based prototype routing to avoid needing task labels at inference. Experiments on MCIT benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance among prompt-based and LoRA-based continual-learning baselines, with code available on GitHub.

The paper characterizes optimal falsification-proof allocation rules under a broad range of falsification technologies and provides an honesty condition under which these rules solve the planner's unconstrained welfare maximization problem. This contributes to mechanism design theory by addressing how to allocate resources without transfers when agents can manipulate their characteristics, which is relevant for designing fair and efficient allocation systems in areas like public housing, school choice, and organ allocation. The paper shows that naively optimal rules lead to falsification and inefficiency, and that optimizing for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification at a heavy cost to agents, generating negative externalities; the characterized rules guard against falsification by least-cost agents and are also optimal for a max-minimizing designer robust to unknown falsification technologies.

**Background**: Mechanism design studies how to design rules (mechanisms) so that self-interested agents achieve desirable outcomes. Non-market allocation refers to allocating resources without using prices or transfers, such as in public housing or school admissions. <a id="item-483"></a>
## [STOPD Accelerates On-Policy Distillation with Random Truncation and IPW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21337) ⭐️ 6.0/10

STOPD randomly truncates student rollouts before generation and uses blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW) to correct the resulting sampling bias, preserving the original on-policy distillation (OPD) training objective. It reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups across multiple teacher-student pairs, task domains, and optimizers. On-policy distillation is computationally expensive due to full rollout generation and per-token teacher feedback, and STOPD provides a principled way to cut this cost without changing the training objective, making OPD more practical for large-scale model training. This could benefit practitioners who distill large language models into smaller deployable students. The method samples a stopping position for each rollout before generation and lets the student generate until that position or natural termination, then applies blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens. The authors prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon optimizers.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a knowledge distillation technique where a student model generates its own token sequences (rollouts) and a teacher model provides token-level feedback on those sequences, reducing the distribution gap between training and inference compared to off-policy distillation on fixed data. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) is a statistical technique that reweights observations by the inverse of their sampling probability to correct for bias when the sampling distribution differs from the target population. STOPD combines these ideas to make OPD more efficient.

## [Location encoders learn administrative boundaries via reverse geocoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24306) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces the first method to learn administrative boundary-aware location encoders by using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal, and proposes a custom architecture called RevGeoRQ that further improves downstream geospatial tasks. This approach explicitly incorporates administrative boundaries and place names into location representations, which are known to strongly influence real-world geospatial phenomena, potentially improving a wide range of geospatial prediction tasks. The method can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their performance; RevGeoRQ uses residual-quantized semantic IDs from reverse-geocoded strings, providing a more interpretable representation, though code and model weights are not yet released.

## [Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting for Sign Language Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24926) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Stable Signer V3 introduces a 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting avatar system for sign language production, adding shared face primitives, identity-specific body deformation, and test-time super-resolution. It reduces facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations. This work advances sign language production by enabling more expressive and accurate avatars, which could improve accessibility tools for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community. It also demonstrates the potential of 4D splatting techniques for high-fidelity, interactive avatar generation beyond sign language. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity, and inference then runs entirely from stored identity parameters, retaining interactive streaming. The system uses TunnelingNet for super-resolution and superquadric primitives for facial expression control.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Gaussian Splatting is a technique for real-time radiance field rendering using point-based primitives, and its deformable 4D variant extends this to dynamic scenes by adding temporal deformation. Sign language production aims to automatically generate sign language animations from text or speech, requiring accurate facial expressions and body movements for intelligibility. Stable Signer V3 builds on this by using 4D deformable primitive splatting to create high-resolution avatars.

## [MC-LDM: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Forecasts Alzheimer's Brain MRI Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25481) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces MC-LDM, a latent diffusion model that uses MRI, tau-PET, CDR, and APOE4 during training but only baseline MRI and metadata at inference to forecast patient-specific 3D brain MRI changes in Alzheimer's progression. Trained on 1,355 visits from 852 ADNI subjects, it reduces average regional volumetric MAE by 18% over the second-best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits. This is the first diffusion-based framework to leverage multimodal priors for MRI forecasting, bridging the gap between rich multimodal supervision and routine clinical deployment where only MRI is available. It enables patient-specific trajectory generation that captures aspects of Alzheimer's heterogeneity not observable from structural anatomy alone. The model fine-tunes a latent diffusion model via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for data-efficient learning and uses auxiliary predictors to estimate unobserved multimodal biomarkers from MRI features and patient covariates, removing the need for tau-PET or CDR at inference. Code is available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 21, 04:00

**Background**: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) perform the diffusion process in a compressed latent space, enabling efficient high-resolution image generation and conditioning. LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes pre-trained weights and injects trainable low-rank matrices. Tau-PET imaging visualizes tau pathology in the brain, providing complementary information to structural MRI for Alzheimer's disease staging.

## [OpenAI improves caching in Codex, Work, and API](https://t.me/ai_newz/4813) ⭐️ 6.0/10

OpenAI has updated its products so that Codex and Work now retain cache persistently, preventing sessions from consuming limits on cache refills after user inactivity. Additionally, the API introduces a 12-hour cache retention option at double the price of the existing 30-minute cache. This change benefits heavy users of Codex and Work by reducing unexpected limit consumption, and gives API developers more flexibility to optimize costs for long-running or intermittent workloads. It reflects a broader industry trend of offering tiered cache retention as a cost-management tool. The 12-hour cache option costs twice as much as the 30-minute cache for cache writes, though read pricing may remain the same; developers should evaluate whether extended retention justifies the higher upfront cost based on their usage patterns.
